effect_mechanism: Across sub-practices pooled together, agroforestry trees and shrubs are reported to add habitat and pest-control value. A tropical-agroforestry review states that live fences, windbreaks and isolated trees may contribute to biodiversity conservation, and that retaining or establishing trees in agricultural land may be a critical component of conservation efforts in fragmented landscapes, with floristic diversity that can be high and a substantial number of animal species able to exploit these habitats for feeding, movement and, in some cases, reproduction [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4]. A meta-analysis of tropical agroforestry studies found natural enemies of pests were significantly more abundant under agroforestry than in controls, as part of a general benefit to natural pest control [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1]. A separate perspective review states that agroforestry is likely to have biodiversity benefits compared to conventional arable, pasture or forestry, though this depends on the variety, abundance and ecological suitability of the tree species used [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3].
conditionality: The same meta-analysis that found more natural enemies also reports, for the diversity (rather than abundance) of natural enemies, that most studies (7 of 11) showed no effect and the response of predation and parasitism was mixed, with 3 of the 7 studies showing no effect and the rest split evenly between positive and negative — held out here as a finding on a narrower measure of the same taxon group, not a contradiction of the abundance result [ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_2]. The review-level units generalise across cited studies rather than measuring anything themselves, and the review qualifies that agroforestry elements 'are not substitutes for the original vegetation' and that almost all its cited studies were in landscapes with some remnant forest nearby, so element value and landscape context are confounded [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4]. None of the four units names a country, income group or farming system for this pooled row, so although the pattern is consistent it only transfers as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_pumarino15_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_3].

effect_mechanism: Linear plantings add woody habitat structure to farmland. A tropical-agroforestry review states that, depending on their floristic diversity, structural complexity and management, windbreaks may help conserve a large number of plant and animal species, including a limited number of forest-dependent species, by providing food, cover from predators, refuge and travel lanes [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_2]. In Colombia and Costa Rica, farmers report that planting live fences increases landscape connectivity, creating local corridors that both fauna and flora can use, which they see as positive for native biodiversity conservation [ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6]. The same review also reports a mixed case: in Queensland, Australia, planted eucalyptus windbreaks were useful habitat for some bird species but insignificant habitat for mammals and rainforest specialists, and held much lower value as wildlife habitat than riparian vegetation, which the authors attribute to the windbreaks' lower structural complexity and single-species planting [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3].
conditionality: The class stays slight because one of the three units finds no added value for mammals and forest specialists relative to riparian habitat, holding agreement at medium rather than high [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3]. None of the three states a size for the conservation gain: the windbreak review is a generalisation across cited temperate studies, the live-fence unit is a farmer-perception survey across Colombia and Costa Rica (upper-middle and high income), and neither names the countries, income group or farming system behind the pooled row, which is why confidence stays low and the row only transfers as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_moran18_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_3].

effect_mechanism: On red and lateritic soils in Jhargram, West Bengal, India, an agri-horti-silviculture system of Gmelina arborea and grafted mango trees with pigeon pea grown in the alleys had the highest earthworm diversity of the systems compared, with a Simpson's diversity index of 0.62 against 0.41 in sole pigeon pea [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. Tree prunings and leaf fall were kept in the field.
conditionality: The strong class rests on a single trial and a single taxon: earthworm diversity is a soil-biodiversity indicator, not a measure of wider farm or landscape biodiversity, and statistical significance of the difference is not reported [ev_biodiversity_outcome_biswas22_1]. The system was fertilised and given need-based irrigation at tree establishment, so the result applies to managed alley systems on degraded lateritic soils in lower-middle-income settings; further studies, on other taxa, are needed before this reads as a general effect.

effect_mechanism: Shade trees over coffee and cocoa hold species that sun plantations lose. A global meta-analysis of coffee and cacao by De Beenhouwer et al. found total species richness fell by 46%, and forest-species richness by 65%, when traditional agroforest under a diverse, mostly indigenous shade canopy was compared with plantation under sparse shade of one or a few tree species; the structurally complex canopy lets more species persist [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_2]. A meta-analysis of cocoa found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry systems than in cocoa monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and a review reports, from Gordon et al. (2007), bird diversity between 120 and 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. In Nicaraguan coffee, most certification schemes had a tree-diversity index, used as a proxy for habitat quality, that rose against non-certified farms [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1].
conditionality: The gains are measured against sun or sparse-shade plantations. Against natural forest, agroforest held 11% fewer species in total and 35% fewer forest species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_4]; that marks a ceiling, since shade cropping replaces plantation or farmland rather than forest, not a loss caused by the practice. The other harm finding is a yield trade-off in Cameroonian cocoa: yields above 1 t/ha did not seem attainable with more than 10 associated species, while about 750 kg/ha was possible with up to 20-23 species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. The bird figure and the Nicaraguan result are second-hand readings, and the review notes the shaded coffee systems had an overall decline in yield [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. justification.mechanism: Shade trees over coffee and cocoa hold species that sun plantations lose. A global meta-analysis of coffee and cacao by De Beenhouwer et al. found total species richness fell by 46%, and forest-species richness by 65%, when traditional agroforest under a diverse, mostly indigenous shade canopy was compared with plantation under sparse shade of one or a few tree species; the structurally complex canopy lets more species persist [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_2]. A meta-analysis of cocoa found a significantly higher number of animal species in agroforestry systems than in cocoa monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1], and a review reports, from Gordon et al. (2007), bird diversity between 120 and 306% higher in three shaded coffee systems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2]. In Nicaraguan coffee, most certification schemes had a tree-diversity index, used as a proxy for habitat quality, that rose against non-certified farms [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1].
justification.conditionality: The gains are measured against sun or sparse-shade plantations. Against natural forest, agroforest held 11% fewer species in total and 35% fewer forest species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_4]; that marks a ceiling, since shade cropping replaces plantation or farmland rather than forest, not a loss caused by the practice. The other harm finding is a yield trade-off in Cameroonian cocoa: yields above 1 t/ha did not seem attainable with more than 10 associated species, while about 750 kg/ha was possible with up to 20-23 species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seghieri19_7]. Scheme design matters: C.A.F.E. Practices was the only Nicaraguan certification scheme under which tree diversity fell [ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. The bird figure and the Nicaraguan result are second-hand readings, and the review notes the shaded coffee systems had an overall decline in yield [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jezeer17_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_castle21s_1]. The coffee and cacao meta-analysis draws on Latin America, Asia and Africa, most of it Latin American [ev_biodiversity_outcome_debeen13_1]; the cocoa meta-analysis draws mainly on lower-middle-income countries [ev_biodiversity_outcome_niether20_1]. The cocoa and coffee units from single crops enter under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling.

effect_mechanism: In Colombian silvopastoral systems, biodiversity rises relative to open pasture, the land use the practice replaces. A global meta-analysis (47 publications, 279 comparisons) found silvopastoral systems supported 28.4% higher biodiversity than open pastures, with native-tree silvopasture raising biodiversity by 36.3% and planted-tree silvopasture by 20.9%, both against open pastures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_12]. Invertebrate abundance showed the largest taxon-specific gain against open pasture, 53.7% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_8]. In Colombia specifically, a World Bank project evaluation reports that silvopastoral systems played a major role in increasing and conserving biodiversity at farm and landscape level, raising the number of species (richness) and individuals observed (abundance), including forest-dependent and endangered species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]; bird monitoring on Colombian cattle farms found intensive silvopasture had four times more birds and 35% higher species richness than grass monocultures, and ant species richness was 62% higher than in treeless pastures in the same landscape [ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_montagnini15_2]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon also significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2]. A tropical-agroforestry review states that pastures with isolated trees generally show higher bird diversity than pastures without them [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1].
conditionality: The same global meta-analysis measures silvopasture against a second, different benchmark — ungrazed native forest — and there the sign reverses: native-tree silvopasture held 18.1% lower overall biodiversity, 14.8% lower plant biodiversity and 24.4% lower invertebrate biodiversity than native forest, with invertebrate abundance 30.2% lower [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_5, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_9, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_11]. This is a conservation benchmark, not the intervention counterfactual: it means silvopasture holds less biodiversity than intact forest, not that converting grazing land to silvopasture reduces biodiversity, so the class is set from the open-pasture comparisons and these forest-benchmark units are held out of it. Two further forest-benchmark comparisons, for birds and bird species richness, found no significant difference, and the invertebrate-abundance gain against open pasture was itself not significant despite a large point estimate [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_6, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_7, ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_10]. The meta-analysis does not report the countries behind its figures, so only the Colombian project evidence anchors this row to the LIC/LMIC target; as a pooled global figure it transfers only as adjacent [ev_biodiversity_outcome_nguyen26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_cmscr20_8]. The bird-diversity review's single worked example compares recently abandoned pasture against actively grazed pasture, so grazing cessation is confounded with the trees themselves [ev_biodiversity_outcome_harv13_1].

effect_mechanism: The carbon evidence splits by sub-practice. Silvopastoral systems read strongest on their own, planted silvoarable and regeneration-based farmland read a moderate gain, and cross-family and linear-boundary readings are only slight — so the roll-up states a moderate gain rather than the pooled slight reading. In Colombia, a World Bank project evaluation reports net accumulated CO2 removals of 1,131,056 t CO2e from converting pasturelands to dispersed trees, live fences and intensive silvopastoral systems [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10], Costa Rican silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg C/ha/yr against below 1 Mg C/ha/yr in treeless pasture [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1], and a global land-use-conversion meta-analysis found soil organic carbon rose 31 to 66% converting agriculture to silvopasture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_39]. In Ethiopia, FMNR-based reforestation projects audited by forestry experts sequestered 181,650 and 94,817 tonnes of CO2 at two sites since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. Under regeneration-based parkland systems, soil carbon is reported 46% higher under Faidherbia albida canopy than outside it in Senegal [ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1], a pan-Sahelian review of shrub and tree parklands found soil total carbon 20 to 75% higher under woody canopies than open fields [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_2], and in Honduras, organic matter content in Quesungual fields rose from 2.4% to 4.5% over four years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates carbon and greenhouse-gas sequestration strongly increased, citing tree-cover gain through afforestation or FMNR as a way to sequester carbon in biomass [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. For linear and cross-family plantings, a review of East African agroforestry found aboveground carbon of 26.7 Mg C/ha held in trees on boundaries [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_5], and a pan-tropical soil study found agroforestry significantly raised soil organic carbon by an overall effect size of 1.21 compared with crop monocultures, with a 40% rise in soil organic carbon, 13% in nitrogen storage and 50% lower soil erosion [ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_2]. The IPCC AR6 AFOLU chapter cites a global technical mitigation potential of 9.4 GtCO2eq/yr for agroforestry [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_3].
conditionality: Almost none of this evidence is a measured net CO2e balance for the practice itself: most of it is modelled regional or global mitigation potential (IPCC, Roe et al.), a carbon stock without a time denominator, or a single-gas figure, which is why confidence stays only medium despite 98 units and high agreement on direction. Held against the pattern, in Niger after four years scattered Ziziphus trees raised soil carbon by 5 to 10% and nitrogen by 10 to 15%, but the differences were not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1], and in Ethiopia soil organic carbon, total nitrogen and other chemical and physical soil properties did not significantly differ under versus outside Faidherbia albida canopy at the end of one season [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1]. Converting existing forest to agroforestry is also measured as a loss in several readings of the same global meta-analysis — not the adoption pathway this cell is about — and the silvopastoral gains sit mostly in upper-middle-income Colombia and high-income Costa Rica, so the row transfers only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target despite the strong Latin American silvopastoral signal [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10].

justification.conditionality: These units come from high-income Costa Rica, from coffee and silvopastoral systems, and the shaded-coffee and silvopasture figures are cited secondary results [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. They lie outside the LIC/LMIC target income band and should not be transferred to LIC/LMIC tree-crop systems without local evidence [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6].

effect_mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings, trees on farms raise both biomass and soil carbon. Across sub-Saharan Africa, agroforestry improved soil organic carbon over controls (RR 1.2) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1]; in West African fields, the presence of shrubs and trees raised soil total C overall, though variably (+ 20 to 75%), ascribed to litter deposition and sediment trapping [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_2]; and a meta-analysis cited for Senegal reports 46 per cent more soil organic carbon under Faidherbia canopy than outside it [ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. East African agroforestry systems stock an average of 24.2 Mg C ha−1 in biomass and 98.8 Mg C ha−1 in the soil, with much of the above-ground carbon held in homegardens, perennial tree-crop systems and trees on boundaries [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muthuri23_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_5]. On degraded lateritic soils in West Bengal, India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea alley system raised soil organic carbon to 0.59% after 10 years, against 0.34% under sole pigeon pea [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. Total biomass carbon in cocoa agroforestry is on average 2.5 times higher than in monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1]. In Ethiopia, regeneration projects at Humbo and Soddo report 181,650 and 94,817 tonnes of CO2 sequestered since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_12]. A multi-country restoration programme observed an overall relative increase of 3% in soil organic carbon over baseline and a significant association between scaling up trees on-farm and gains in soil organic carbon [ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_4]. Modelled regional potentials put agroforestry at 0.19 GtCO2eq yr−1 in Africa and the Middle East and 0.37 GtCO2eq yr−1 in Asia and the developing Pacific at up to $100/tCO2eq [ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_3]. In Lempira, Honduras, soil organic matter under the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system, monitored for four years in three places, increased from 2.4% to 4.5% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].
conditionality: On-farm measurements are mixed: soil organic C did not differ significantly under and outside Faidherbia albida canopies in Ethiopia [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1]; at Sadore in Niger, soil cropped with Ziziphus mauritiana trees held 5 to 10% more soil organic carbon than soil cropped without them, but the difference was not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]; in Malawi soil C under a Tephrosia intercrop was 1.57 against 1.46 under monoculture maize, a trend with P value = 0.10 [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]; cocoa agroforestry showed no significant differences in soil chemical properties from monoculture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_niether20_1]; and certified shade coffee in Nicaragua had positive but not statistically significant impacts on above-ground carbon stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_castle21s_1]. The pooled size rests on soil organic carbon response ratios, a component of sequestration [ev_soil_organic_carbon_kuyah19_1]. The Kenyan WOCAT rating is a compiler judgement, not a measured stock [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. The Honduran figure is soil organic matter used as a proxy for soil organic carbon, measured before and after on the same plots with no concurrent slash-and-burn control; it comes from a promoter-written grey-literature article, and the system bundles the trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].

effect_mechanism: Across several independent global meta-analyses of soil organic carbon (SOC) under agroforestry, trees replacing cropland consistently raise SOC. A meta-analysis of paired agroforestry-versus-adjacent-cropland/pasture studies found agroforestry held soil C stocks of 126 Mg C/ha, 19% more than cropland or pasture, driven by litter from tree pruning and herbaceous root inputs [ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_1]. A separate paired-comparison meta-analysis found agroforestry increased SOC stocks by an average of 25.9% (95% CI 17.4–34.4%), with a greater gain when trees were established in cropland than in pasture, and converting cropland specifically to agroforestry generally increased SOC storage [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]. A meta-analysis built for IPCC Tier 1 coefficients found a mean stock-change factor of 1.25 for cropland converted to agroforestry [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_1]. A fourth, larger land-use-conversion meta-analysis found SOC stocks rose significantly converting agriculture to agroforestry, by 26%, 40% and 34% at different sampling depths, and from pasture/grassland to agroforestry by 9% and 10% at different depths [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_12, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_29, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_11, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_19]. By specific agroforestry type, the same meta-analysis found agriculture-to-agrisilviculture gains of 10 to 40% depending on depth, agriculture-to-agrosilvopastoral gains of 21 to 30%, and agriculture-to-silvopasture gains of 31 to 66% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_15, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_34, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_7, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_26, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_35, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_39, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27].
conditionality: Set against these gains, converting existing forest to agroforestry instead loses SOC: the IPCC-coefficient meta-analysis found a stock-change factor of 0.89 for forest converted to agroforestry (less than the cropland factor of 1.25, indicating a loss rather than a gain) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_2], and the land-use-conversion meta-analysis found forest-to-agroforestry losses of 22%, and by type, 12% for agrisilviculture and 44% for silvopasture [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_11, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_7]. Converting uncultivated or degraded land also sometimes lost SOC — 23% for agroforestry generally and 47% for silvopasture specifically — which the authors attribute to the heterogeneity of that counterfactual category (bare land, degraded land and no-tree controls pooled together), and converting pasture to agrisilviculture lost 11%, attributed by the authors to the loss of perennial-grass root inputs once trees replace grass [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_20, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_40, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_36]. Two further independent meta-analyses agree that converting pasture specifically (rather than cropland) to agroforestry often shows no significant SOC change, because perennial pasture grass already supplies large belowground carbon inputs that dominate the soil carbon pool whether or not trees are added, and silvopasture had the smallest or no increase in soil carbon of any agroforestry type for the same reason [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_cardinael18_3]. The land-use-conversion meta-analysis itself reports null results at several depths for pasture, forest-plantation and uncultivated-land conversions, and even finds no significant SOC influence from any land-use conversion to agroforestry at its deepest sampled profile [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_3, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_8, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_9, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_22, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_23, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_31, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_32, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_33, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_41]. None of these four meta-analyses lists the countries or income groups behind its pooled estimate, so the row is scoped as mixed income context rather than tied directly to the LIC/LMIC target, though the land-use-conversion study notes its base spans multiple countries across the Americas, Africa and Asia [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_1].

effect_mechanism: Trees on rainfed cropland add carbon to the soil, mainly under their canopies, through litter and root inputs on soils depleted by annual cropping. A meta-analysis of semi-arid West Africa found that shrubs and trees on agricultural fields raised soil total carbon by 20 to 75%, an effect ascribed to litter deposition and sediment trapping under the canopies of woody perennials [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_2]. A global meta-analysis found that converting cropland to agroforestry generally increased soil organic carbon storage [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]. An FAO review for Senegal cites a meta-analysis by Sileshi (2016) that soil under the canopy of Faidherbia albida holds on average 46 per cent more organic carbon than soil outside it [ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. In a 10-year field experiment on degraded lateritic soil in West Bengal, India, soil organic carbon reached 0.59% under a Gmelina–mango–pigeon pea system against 0.34% under sole pigeon pea, from 0.30% at the start [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. In southern Malawi, soil carbon showed a trend upward with a Tephrosia relay intercrop, 1.57 against 1.46 under monoculture maize (P value = 0.10) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]. In Lempira, Honduras, soil organic matter under the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system, monitored for four years in three places, increased from 2.4% to 4.5% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].
conditionality: Not every field trial finds the gain. In Ethiopia's Central Rift Valley, soil organic carbon did not significantly differ under and outside the canopy of Faidherbia albida at the end of the 2013 season [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1], and in Niger, after four years, the block with Ziziphus trees held 5 to 10 % more soil organic carbon than the block without, a difference that was not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. What separates the results, as far as the evidence says, is time and where the carbon is measured: the large gains are under canopies or after a decade of tree growth [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1], while the null results come from single seasons or a few years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. Under-canopy figures do not scale to the whole field: the parkland comparisons set soil under the tree against soil outside it, so the field-level gain depends on how much of the field the canopies cover [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. Most of the evidence is from low- and lower-middle-income West Africa, Ethiopia, Malawi and India, within the LIC/LMIC target. The Honduran figure is soil organic matter used as a proxy for soil organic carbon, measured before and after on the same plots with no concurrent slash-and-burn control; it comes from a promoter-written grey-literature article, and the system bundles the trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].

The IPCC AR6 AFOLU chapter cites a global analysis estimating agroforestry's technical mitigation potential at 9.4 GtCO2eq/yr, and further estimates a technical potential of 4.1 (0.3–9.4) GtCO2eq/yr for 2020-2050, of which 0.8 (0.4–1.1) GtCO2eq/yr is available at USD100/tCO2 [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_5]. A regional modelling study finds agroforestry's mitigation density about 45 tCO2eq/ha, and across the Africa-Middle East region its cost-effective mitigation potential at 0.19 GtCO2eq/yr (8% of the regional total) [ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_2]. In Brazil, a review reports agroforestry carbon sequestration rates varying by climate from 954 to 3670 tCO2/km2/yr, with a technical potential of 0.1 to 5.7 GtCO2eq/yr, the largest among the land uses it compared [ev_carbon_sequestration_santos25_3]. One directly measured finding in the row combines biomass and soil carbon sequestration with changes in net CH4 and N2O emissions and estimates a shift to agroforestry can mitigate 27.2 t CO2eq/ha/yr, at least over the early growth stage up to an average age of 14 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_1]. The Regreening Africa endline survey found a relative 3% increase in soil organic carbon compared with baseline, with significant variation across countries and sites [ev_soil_organic_carbon_rgaf23_2].
justification.conditionality: Only one of these 67 units — the biomass-plus-soil-plus-gas estimate above — is a measured net balance for the practice itself; the rest are modelled regional or global mitigation potentials, single-gas or stock-only figures, or review restatements of other studies, so the engine cannot let most of them set the class, which is why confidence stays very low despite the consistent direction. A further eight units are held out because their comparator is existing natural forest, not the farming system the practice would actually replace: converting forest to agroforestry lost soil organic carbon in every reading — 22 to 26% at shallow depth and 24% for agrisilviculture specifically — and forest-to-silvopastoral/agrosilvopastoral conversions likewise lost 27 to 36% at various depths, reversals that describe deforestation for agroforestry, not the cropland- or pasture-to-agroforestry adoption pathway this cell is about [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_10, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_14, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_25, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_37]. None of the global modelling or meta-analysis units names the countries behind its pooled estimate, so the row transfers only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target rather than being confidently in context [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipccar6_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_roe21_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_muchane20_1].

effect_mechanism: Trees planted into cropland add carbon to the soil through leaf litter, prunings and roots, raising soil carbon storage above that of the crop grown alone. In a ten-year trial on degraded red and lateritic soil in West Bengal, India, soil organic carbon under a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea alley system reached 0.59% against 0.34% under sole pigeon pea, from an initial 0.30% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. A global meta-analysis found that converting cropland to agroforestry generally increased soil carbon storage, consistent with earlier syntheses [ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3]. In southern Malawi, Tephrosia vogelii relay-planted under maize keeps growing into the dry season and returns nitrogen-rich leafy residues; at Songani soil C under this intercrop was 1.57 against 1.46 under monoculture maize [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1].
conditionality: The direction is consistent, but not every site shows a clear gain. The Malawi difference was a trend that was not significant (P value = 0.10) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1], and at Sadore, Niger, the block with Ziziphus mauritiana trees held from 5 to 10 % more soil organic carbon than the block without after four years of millet and cowpea, a difference that was not significant [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. The Niger trial compares two blocks with tree presence neither randomised nor replicated, so block differences are mixed into the contrast [ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1]. Soil carbon is a component of carbon removal, measured here as a stock or concentration, not as a removal rate, and tree biomass storage is not counted in this row [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1]. The strongest gain comes from a long-running research-station trial on degraded soil, where the starting carbon was low [ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1]. The field evidence is from low-income Malawi and Niger and lower-middle-income India, all rainfed cropping; the meta-analysis is global [ev_soil_organic_carbon_snapp10_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_bado21_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_biswas22_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_3].

effect_mechanism: In Sudano-Sahelian cropland, shrubs and trees on agricultural fields had an overall positive but variable effect on soil total carbon (+ 20 to 75%), and a cited meta-analysis reports that soil under Faidherbia albida canopy holds on average 46 per cent more organic carbon than outside it [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. The externally audited Humbo FMNR project in Ethiopia reports CO2 sequestered since 2007 [ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler adds that increasing tree cover through FMNR is one of the ways to sequester carbon in biomass [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. In Lempira, Honduras, soil organic matter under the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system, monitored for four years in three places, increased from 2.4% to 4.5% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].
conditionality: Two literature units measure soil carbon under trees (a component of sequestration), and the Humbo figure is a project total from a World Vision self-evaluation with no per-hectare or per-year denominator [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. The literature is from semi-arid West Africa and Ethiopia (low- and lower-middle-income countries) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_felix18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wvfmnr19_11]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not a measured stock or rate [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_507_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Measured directly on Ethiopian wheat farms, soil organic C did not differ significantly under and outside the Faidherbia albida canopy at the end of the 2013 cropping season, so the cited 46 per cent canopy gain was not reproduced at that site; this null lowers the agreement rather than the class [ev_soil_organic_carbon_sida18_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_faosen24_1]. The Honduran figure is soil organic matter used as a proxy for soil organic carbon, measured before and after on the same plots with no concurrent slash-and-burn control; it comes from a promoter-written grey-literature article, and the system bundles the trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning [ev_soil_organic_carbon_welc02_3].

effect_mechanism: Thirteen units speak to carbon in shaded perennial-crop systems (coffee, cocoa, coconut), though none gives a net CO2e sequestration rate. A multi-country cocoa meta-analysis found total biomass carbon stock 2.5 times higher under agroforestry than monoculture [ev_carbon_sequestration_niether20_1], while finding no significant difference in soil organic carbon between the two systems [ev_soil_organic_carbon_niether20_1]. A review of East African systems found aboveground carbon stocks of 29.9 Mg C/ha in perennial tree-crop systems [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4], and modelled Ethiopian enset-coffee systems at 96.6 to 153.4 Mg/ha of biomass carbon [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_6]. In Costa Rica, an eight-year eddy-covariance study measured a mean carbon storage of 3.6 t C/ha/yr in coffee agroforestry [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5], and a separate Costa Rican comparison found 29.8 Mg/ha more aboveground biomass carbon in shaded coffee than in full-sun plantations [ev_carbon_sequestration_villa20_6]. In Kerala, India, a review reports carbon storage in mixed coconut stands clearly greater than in sole coconut stands, and higher soil carbon sequestration for coconut intercropped with fruit trees than sole coconut [ev_carbon_sequestration_kumar22_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_kumar22_1]. In Nicaragua, certified shade-coffee schemes (C.A.F.E. Practices, Fairtrade, Organic, Rainforest Alliance, Utz) all had positive impacts on aboveground carbon stocks compared with non-certified coffee, though not statistically significant [ev_carbon_sequestration_castle21s_1]. A review states agroforestry can improve soil organic matter by 20 to 35% [ev_soil_organic_carbon_patil25_5].
conditionality: This cell is data deficient: every one of the thirteen units is a carbon stock without a time denominator, a crop-specific modelled or cited-secondary figure, a non-significant result, or a single-gas figure rather than a measured net CO2e balance for the practice. Against the carbon gains above, a global synthesis found net soil CH4 emissions increased with a shift from agriculture to shaded perennial-crop systems — the opposite of the reduction seen for other agroforestry types — attributed to nitrogen from nitrogen-fixing shade trees inhibiting CH4 oxidation, though the authors note the difference was relatively small [ev_carbon_sequestration_kim16_4]. In Sumatra, shaded coffee with a leguminous shade canopy had soil N2O emissions five times higher than open-grown coffee and about half the soil CH4 uptake [ev_carbon_sequestration_verc07_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_verc07_2]. The Costa Rican eddy-covariance figure is the one directly measured carbon-balance number in the row, but it is a single farm over one study period, not independently replicated, so nothing here reaches the bar for a class [ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5]. The evidence spans low/lower-middle-income East African and Indian coffee/coconut systems through high-income Costa Rican coffee and upper-middle-income Indonesian coffee, so even once a class becomes available it would only transfer as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_carbon_sequestration_muthuri23_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_kumar22_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_seghieri19_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_verc07_1].

effect_mechanism: In Colombia and Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems are reported to raise carbon stocks and sequestration. The World Bank's Colombian Conservation and Sustainable Development of the Coffee Growing Regions project reports net accumulated CO2 removals of 1,131,056 t CO2e from converting pasturelands to dispersed trees in pasture, live fences, intensive silvopastoral systems and secondary-forest conservation [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10]. In Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg C/ha/yr, against below 1 Mg C/ha/yr in treeless pasture [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. A global meta-analysis of land-use conversions found soil organic carbon stocks rose 66% and 31% at different depths converting agriculture to silvopasture, 17% converting forest plantation to silvopasture, and 32% converting forest to silvopasture at the deepest sampled profile, where the authors note silvopasture held more SOC than the forest it replaced at that depth [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_39, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_24, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_38]. A Colombian review states a preliminary GHG balance where lower nitrogen losses and greater carbon capture in intensive silvopastoral systems offset livestock methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2], and silvopastoral systems built from degraded natural woodland are reported to mitigate climate change by increasing above- and below-ground carbon stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4]. Among pasture-improvement practices assessed in a Colombian climate-smart-agriculture matrix, only tree-improved pastures and live fences showed a positive effect on the mitigation pillar [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon also significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties, retaining forest carbon [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2].
conditionality: Set against this, the same global meta-analysis found soil organic carbon fell 44% converting forest to silvopasture at a shallower sampled depth (against the 32% gain reported at the deepest profile) and fell 47% converting uncultivated or other land to silvopasture — a reversal the engine counts as measured harm, which the authors attribute to the heterogeneity of the uncultivated/other category (bare, degraded or control land) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_6, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_40]. Converting pasture or grassland to silvopasture showed no noticeable change in soil organic carbon in the same meta-analysis, and two further global meta-analyses likewise found no significant effect of converting pasture to agroforestry on soil carbon, attributing it to perennial grass roots already dominating belowground carbon inputs before trees are added [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_9, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3]. The forest-to-silvopasture figures are measured against existing natural forest, a conservation benchmark, not the pasture-to-silvopasture adoption counterfactual that matters for the practice's climate-mitigation role. justification.mechanism: In Colombia and Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems are reported to raise carbon stocks and sequestration. The World Bank's Colombian Conservation and Sustainable Development of the Coffee Growing Regions project reports net accumulated CO2 removals of 1,131,056 t CO2e from converting pasturelands to dispersed trees in pasture, live fences, intensive silvopastoral systems and secondary-forest conservation [ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10]. In Costa Rica, silvopastoral systems had a carbon storage potential of 1.2 to 4.5 Mg C/ha/yr, against below 1 Mg C/ha/yr in treeless pasture [ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1]. A global meta-analysis of land-use conversions found soil organic carbon stocks rose 66% and 31% at different depths converting agriculture to silvopasture, 17% converting forest plantation to silvopasture, and 32% converting forest to silvopasture at the deepest sampled profile, where the authors note silvopasture held more SOC than the forest it replaced at that depth [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_39, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_24, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_38]. A Colombian review states a preliminary GHG balance where lower nitrogen losses and greater carbon capture in intensive silvopastoral systems offset livestock methane emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_murg13_2], and silvopastoral systems built from degraded natural woodland are reported to mitigate climate change by increasing above- and below-ground carbon stocks [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_4]. Among pasture-improvement practices assessed in a Colombian climate-smart-agriculture matrix, only tree-improved pastures and live fences showed a positive effect on the mitigation pillar [ev_carbon_sequestration_taboada20_6]. Properties with silvopastoral intervention in the Colombian Amazon also significantly reduced deforestation rates compared with control properties, retaining forest carbon [ev_landscape_forest_cover_bur24_2].
justification.conditionality: Set against this, the same global meta-analysis found soil organic carbon fell 44% converting forest to silvopasture at a shallower sampled depth (against the 32% gain reported at the deepest profile) and fell 47% converting uncultivated or other land to silvopasture — a reversal the engine counts as measured harm, which the authors attribute to the heterogeneity of the uncultivated/other category (bare, degraded or control land) [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_6, ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_40]. Converting pasture or grassland to silvopasture showed no noticeable change in soil organic carbon in the same meta-analysis, and two further global meta-analyses likewise found no significant effect of converting pasture to agroforestry on soil carbon, attributing it to perennial grass roots already dominating belowground carbon inputs before trees are added [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_9, ev_soil_organic_carbon_ma20_4, ev_soil_organic_carbon_shi18_3]. The forest-to-silvopasture figures are measured against existing natural forest, a conservation benchmark, not the pasture-to-silvopasture adoption counterfactual that matters for the practice's climate-mitigation role. All of this is global meta-analysis evidence without a Colombia/Costa Rica-specific breakdown, so only the World Bank project and Costa Rican figures anchor the row to its stated countries; as pooled global findings the SOC units transfer only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_organic_carbon_dest18_27, ev_carbon_sequestration_cmscr20_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_montagnini15_1].

effect_mechanism: Trees change how much rain reaches groundwater and streams in opposite ways. On the recharge side, the IPCC assessment states that agroforestry increases groundwater recharge in drylands when managed at moderate density (Ilstedt et al. 2016; Bargués-Tobella et al. 2020) [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ipccar6_1], and, combining canopy interception and transpiration data of trees with their effects on water infiltration, Ilstedt et al. derived an optimal intermediate tree density for parklands from a groundwater-recharge perspective [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_vannoordwijk21_6]. On the water-use side, a review cites Wallace et al. (2005): because agroforestry systems include a share of trees, they use more water than pure agricultural systems, though less than full-cover forest, leaving less water to feed groundwater and maintain dry-season streamflow [ev_water_yield_zhu19_1]. Groundwater recharge is used here as a component of catchment water yield.
conditionality: Studies disagree, and what separates them is the balance between higher tree water use and better infiltration, which tree density sets. effect_mechanism: Trees on farms slightly reduce the damage drought does to farm households. In Isiolo County communities in Kenya, households rated agroforestry important during drought, a farmer said deep-rooted mango trees get water from deep down, others said trees do not dry up fast and keep producing fruit when there is no rain, and 74% of respondents had planted trees with drought in mind; the study concludes that agroforestry can and does build livelihood resilience to drought [ev_t3_drought_importance_quandt17_8, ev_t3_drought_deeproots_quandt17_7, ev_t3_drought_farmerquote_quandt17_12, ev_t3_drought_intentional_quandt17_14, ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10]. Reviews report that under drought understorey crop yields could be higher than in an open system even in intense shade, that trees were the most important source of animal food and milk for Zambian agro-pastoralists during drought (Chibinga et al. 2012), that live fences supply livestock fodder when pasture is scarce, and that agroforestry biomass production varied less over 4 years than conventional systems in semi-arid Brazil, attributed mainly to water availability (Martins et al. 2013) [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14, ev_drought_hazard_moran18_1, ev_drought_hazard_santos25_6]. In an eastern Canadian soybean intercrop, experimentally induced drought caused crop losses in the monocrop only (Nasielski et al. 2015) [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet rates drought impacts as reduced, its compiler judging that FMNR improves micro-climate and soil moisture and therefore mitigates the impact of droughts [ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. In Lempira, Honduras, a practitioner article on the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system reports that, compared with farmers who remained with slash-and-burn, Quesungual farmers did not experience a total loss in maize production during the dry period of El Niño in 1997, which the authors put down to improved soil conditions [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].
conditionality: Effects are not uniform, and for some adopters the trees made drought losses worse. During the extreme drought of 2015/16 in Ghana, a field study found that all cocoa plants under Albizia ferruginea shade trees died and cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria suffered 77% mortality, while cocoa in full sun kept higher sap flux; soil water content was higher in full sun, which the authors link to competition for water in the shaded systems [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. Elsewhere, a review says tree shade could decrease understorey yields under normal rainfall, and the Senegal review reports no clear consensus on windbreaks in drought, some studies finding higher yields in drier years and others harm to rainfed crops [ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_13, ev_drought_hazard_faosen24_17]. In Kenya the link between agroforestry and perceived drought held in Burat but not in Kinna, and one Kenyan unit states only that agroforestry has been proposed for resilience [ev_t3_drought_perception_quandt17_5, ev_t3_drought_lh_quandt17_1]. Few units give a size, so the class is slight. Most units are reviews repeating earlier studies or household perception, the Canadian trial is high-income evidence, and the Kenyan FMNR unit is a practitioner judgement on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_drought_hazard_ipccar6ch5_4, ev_drought_hazard_wocat_507_2019_drought_impacts]. The household and fodder evidence comes largely from lower-middle-income Kenya and low-income Zambia, inside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_t3_drought_conclusion_quandt17_10, ev_drought_hazard_dobhal24_14]. The Honduran account is grey literature written by staff of the project that promoted the Quesungual system, so it may overstate the benefit; it does not say how severe the 1997 dry period was, and the trees come bundled with mulching, zero tillage, direct sowing and no burning, so the result cannot be credited to the trees alone [ev_drought_hazard_welc02_2].

effect_mechanism: In a cocoa plantation in Ghana's Ashanti region, shade trees competed with cocoa for soil water through the extreme 2015/16 El Niño drought. All cocoa plants under the recommended leguminous shade tree Albizia ferruginea died; cocoa under Antiaris toxicaria, the most common shade tree, suffered 77% mortality and massive stress, with sap flux density cut to 115 g cm2 day1 against 170 in full sun; and sap-flux recovery after the drought was 163 in full sun against 37 under Antiaris. Soil water content was higher in full sun than under the shade trees, which the authors link to strong competition for soil water [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1].
conditionality: This is a single measured study on a single farm with a few replicate shade trees per species, so the row gives a direction only, with no size class [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. The shade-tree species is part of the result: the loss was total under Albizia and heavy under Antiaris, so other shade species, densities or pruning regimes may behave differently. The drought was extreme; the same plots were also measured through wet and normal dry periods, which separates the drought response from ordinary shade effects [ev_drought_hazard_abdul18_1]. The finding is crop-specific (cocoa) and enters under the shaded-perennial crop-scope ruling; Ghana is lower-middle income, within the LIC/LMIC target. A financed shade-cocoa system in a drought-prone area carries this as a risk to the planted asset and the crop.

effect_mechanism: Across contexts, agroforestry raises household food security mainly through tree products adding to diets and smoothing shortfalls. In Malawi, fertilizer-tree adopters had food crop value 35% higher than non-adopters, driving greater food security [ev_t6_foodsec_ferttree_castle21_8]. In Kenya, agrosilvopastoral extension advice raised the household dietary diversity score by 1.22 points and the number of food groups consumed by 2.291, out of 12 analysed [ev_food_security_castle21s_1]. In Zambia, improved fallows raised the number of months per year with enough grown food by 1.069 months [ev_food_security_castle21s_3]. Across the Regreening Africa endline survey (Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Mali, Niger, Rwanda, Senegal, Somalia), the share of respondents meeting the minimum-dietary-diversity cut-off rose from 16 to 21%, a 31% relative increase, and households that intensified tree-product use saw significant dietary-diversity gains in Ethiopia, Ghana, Niger, Rwanda and Senegal [ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_rgaf23_10]. A World Vision multi-country meta-analysis found project participants' months of food shortage significantly lower, by 0.26 months, than non-participants [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9]. In Senegal, only 3% of FMNR adopters failed to meet annual food needs for more than 4 months against 14% of non-adopters in one zone, and 0% versus 4% in another [ev_food_security_seghieri19_13]. In Nepal, the share of households food-sufficient rose from 52% to 69% after a market-oriented agroforestry intervention, a highly significant change [ev_food_security_pandit19_1], and in Tanzania, improved agroforestry secured enough food year-round for 40% of households against 18% on traditional farms [ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. In Kenya, fruit from on-farm trees was some farmers' only steady food source during the floods, and agroforestry-project households used fewer detrimental coping strategies during the drought and flood hunger periods that followed [ev_food_security_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2]. In Rwanda, a positive association between tree density and food security was found in two of six agroecologies [ev_food_security_ndoli21_1]. Reviews summarise the same mechanism: the IPCC AR6 chapter links increased food security and household income to diversification of production avoiding trade-offs between crop and tree products [ev_food_security_ipccar6ch5_7], and a review states agroforestry could help up to 1.3 billion people on degrading agricultural land in food-security terms [ev_food_security_ipccsrccl6_6]. A synthesis across East African studies names fodder, food, firewood and income as the main livelihood benefits, diversifying livelihoods and acting as safety nets in times of climate shocks [ev_food_security_muthuri23_1].
conditionality: Against this, the same Rwandan study found the opposite in a third agroecology, with increasing tree density associated with lower food security in the Buberuka Highlands even as it raised food security in Congo Nile — measured harm for some households [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. Several units find no effect: Kenyan improved fallow showed no significant nutritional results [ev_food_security_castle21s_2], the Regreening Africa endline's food-insecurity-experience-scale score showed no substantial change [ev_food_security_rgaf23_9], Nigerien FMNR did not reduce months of perceived food shortage though it raised crop diversity [ev_food_security_haglund11_1], and the Sahel food-consumption-score gains were not statistically significant under the authors' own convention, though the authors describe them as increases [ev_food_security_bina15_7, ev_food_security_bina15_8, ev_food_security_bina15_9]. The Talensi and Nepali/Tanzanian gains come from before-and-after project self-evaluations or non-randomised comparisons with no control group, and the World Vision multi-country brief and the Nguyen review both note their findings cannot be fully disentangled from other project activities or, in the review's case, were guaranteed by its own inclusion rule (only studies already showing a food-security improvement were selected) [ev_food_security_talensi21_3, ev_food_security_talensi21_4, ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9, ev_food_security_nguy24n_1]. Most units describe direction without a size; where sizes are given (Malawi, Regreening Africa), the gains sit in low and lower-middle-income African and South Asian contexts, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_t6_foodsec_ferttree_castle21_8, ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_pandit19_1].

justification.mechanism: Across contexts, agroforestry raises household food security mainly through tree products adding to diets and smoothing shortfalls. In Malawi, fertilizer-tree adopters had food crop value 35% higher than non-adopters, driving greater food security [ev_t6_foodsec_ferttree_castle21_8]. In Kenya, agrosilvopastoral extension advice raised the household dietary diversity score by 1.22 points and the number of food groups consumed by 2.291, out of 12 analysed [ev_food_security_castle21s_1]. In Zambia, improved fallows raised the number of months per year with enough grown food by 1.069 months [ev_food_security_castle21s_3]. Across the Regreening Africa endline survey (Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Mali, Niger, Rwanda, Senegal, Somalia), the share of respondents meeting the minimum-dietary-diversity cut-off rose from 16 to 21%, a 31% relative increase, and households that intensified tree-product use saw significant dietary-diversity gains in Ethiopia, Ghana, Niger, Rwanda and Senegal [ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_rgaf23_10]. A World Vision multi-country meta-analysis found project participants' months of food shortage significantly lower, by 0.26 months, than non-participants [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9]. In Senegal, only 3% of FMNR adopters failed to meet annual food needs for more than 4 months against 14% of non-adopters in one zone, and 0% versus 4% in another [ev_food_security_seghieri19_13]. In Nepal, the share of households food-sufficient rose from 52% to 69% after a market-oriented agroforestry intervention, a highly significant change [ev_food_security_pandit19_1], and in Tanzania, improved agroforestry secured enough food year-round for 40% of households against 18% on traditional farms [ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. In Kenya, fruit from on-farm trees was some farmers' only steady food source during the floods, and agroforestry-project households used fewer detrimental coping strategies during the drought and flood hunger periods that followed [ev_food_security_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2]. In Rwanda, a positive association between tree density and food security was found in two of six agroecologies [ev_food_security_ndoli21_1]. Reviews summarise the same mechanism: the IPCC AR6 chapter links increased food security and household income to diversification of production avoiding trade-offs between crop and tree products [ev_food_security_ipccar6ch5_7], and a review states agroforestry could help up to 1.3 billion people on degrading agricultural land in food-security terms [ev_food_security_ipccsrccl6_6]. A synthesis across East African studies names fodder, food, firewood and income as the main livelihood benefits, diversifying livelihoods and acting as safety nets in times of climate shocks [ev_food_security_muthuri23_1].
justification.conditionality: Against this, the same Rwandan study found the opposite in a third agroecology, with increasing tree density associated with lower food security in the Buberuka Highlands even as it raised food security in Congo Nile — measured harm for some households [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. Several units find no effect: Kenyan improved fallow showed no significant nutritional results [ev_food_security_castle21s_2], the Regreening Africa endline's food-insecurity-experience-scale score showed no substantial change [ev_food_security_rgaf23_9], Nigerien FMNR did not reduce months of perceived food shortage though it raised crop diversity [ev_food_security_haglund11_1], and the Sahel food-consumption-score gains were not statistically significant under the authors' own convention, though the authors describe them as increases [ev_food_security_bina15_7, ev_food_security_bina15_8, ev_food_security_bina15_9]. The Talensi and Nepali/Tanzanian gains come from before-and-after project self-evaluations or non-randomised comparisons with no control group, and the World Vision multi-country brief and the Nguyen review both note their findings cannot be fully disentangled from other project activities or, in the review's case, were guaranteed by its own inclusion rule (only studies already showing a food-security improvement were selected) [ev_food_security_talensi21_3, ev_food_security_talensi21_4, ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9, ev_food_security_nguy24n_1]. Most units describe direction without a size; where sizes are given (Malawi, Regreening Africa), the gains sit in low and lower-middle-income African and South Asian contexts, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_t6_foodsec_ferttree_castle21_8, ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_pandit19_1].

effect_mechanism: Across mixed crop–livestock systems, agroforestry raises food security through added food sources and income. In Nepal, the share of households that were food-sufficient rose from 146 of 279 (52%) before a market-oriented agroforestry intervention to 192 of 279 (69%) after, a highly significant change [ev_food_security_pandit19_1]. In Tanzania, improved agroforestry was securing enough food throughout the year for 40% of households, against 18% of households on traditional farms [ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. In the Sahel, moving from low-intensity to young-level farmer-managed natural regeneration raised the household food consumption score by about 12% across Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger and Senegal [ev_food_security_bina15_7]. In Kenya, during floods, some farmers reported fruit from their on-farm trees as their only steady source of food while other crops were underwater or washed away, and agroforestry-project households used fewer detrimental coping strategies (such as consuming seed stock or selling oxen) during the drought and flood hunger periods that followed than a control group [ev_food_security_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_thorlak12_2]. In Rwanda, a positive association between tree density and food security was found in two of six agroecologies [ev_food_security_ndoli21_1].
conditionality: Against this, the same Rwandan study found the opposite in a third agroecology: increasing tree density was associated with lower food security in the Buberuka Highlands, even as it raised the probability of food security in Congo Nile — the practice worsening the outcome for some households, which the engine counts as measured harm [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. The Sahelian gain from low to continuous FMNR showed no significant food-consumption-score gain in any country, and a separate measure, months with a household food deficit, found no significant effect for any FMNR intensity, though the authors read the communities as more resilient during food shortages as an inference rather than a measured result [ev_food_security_bina15_8, ev_food_security_bina15_9]. The Nepali and Tanzanian gains come from before-and-after or non-randomised comparisons with no control group, and the Tanzanian 'improved' farms were also larger, more often in the highlands and kept more dairy cattle and off-farm income, so some of the gain is not attributable to the trees alone [ev_food_security_pandit19_1, ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. All units sit in low and lower-middle-income Sub-Saharan African and South Asian mixed crop–livestock systems, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_food_security_bina15_7, ev_food_security_pandit19_1, ev_food_security_reyes05_1].

effect_mechanism: IPCC assessments link agroforestry to food security through diversification of production that avoids trade-offs between crop and tree products, and an East African systematic review finds that the fodder, food, firewood and income from agroforestry act as safety nets in climate shocks [ev_food_security_ipccar6ch5_7, ev_food_security_muthuri23_1]. The IPCC land report estimates that up to 1.3 billion people on degrading land could benefit in food security through agroforestry [ev_food_security_ipccsrccl6_6]. Under Regreening Africa the share of respondents consuming at least five of the ten food items rose from 16 to 21, a 31 percent increase, and households that intensified their use of tree products saw significant gains in dietary diversity [ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_rgaf23_10]. In the Nepal mid-hills the share of food-sufficient households rose from 52% to 69% after a market-oriented agroforestry project [ev_food_security_pandit19_1]. In Nyando, Kenya, agroforestry-project households used fewer detrimental coping strategies in hunger periods and some relied on tree fruit when floods washed crops away, and in Rwanda tree density was associated with higher food security in some agroecologies [ev_food_security_thorlak12_2, ev_food_security_thorlak12_1, ev_food_security_ndoli21_1]. A global review of nature-based solutions for food security cites population-survey studies finding better food access where agroforestry was applied in southern Africa, Brazil and China over periods of up to 20 years [ev_food_security_nguy24n_1]. A systematic review of agroforestry adoption in sub-Saharan Africa, mostly from Ethiopia, Kenya and Malawi, finds that agroforestry recurrently enhances dietary diversity, particularly where fruit- and vegetable-producing trees are included [ev_food_security_jemaneh26_1]. In the East Usambara Mountains, Tanzania, improved agroforestry secured enough food throughout the year for 40% of households against 18% of households using traditional practices [ev_food_security_reyes05_1].
conditionality: Few units say how big the effect is, so the class is capped at moderate. In Rwanda's Buberuka Highlands more trees went with lower food security, a measured harm, while in Congo Nile the association ran the other way [ev_food_security_ndoli21_2]. The Regreening Africa FIES score showed no substantial change, moving from 4.9 to 4.8, and the Campbell systematic review found the impact on nutrition and food security beneficial or neutral across the studies it covered [ev_food_security_rgaf23_9, ev_food_security_castle21s_4]. The Regreening Africa and Nepal results are before-and-after surveys with no control group, and the Nepal project bundled the trees with market linkage, training, subsidies and organic fertiliser [ev_food_security_rgaf23_8, ev_food_security_pandit19_1]. The Tanzanian comparison is a household survey without randomisation: the improved farms bundled trees with cash crops, manure and dairy cattle, were larger and had more off-farm income, so part of the food-sufficiency gap is a livestock and wealth effect [ev_food_security_reyes05_1]. The sub-Saharan review notes that outcomes vary with agroforestry type, complementary practices and the wider context, and gives no pooled food-security estimate [ev_food_security_jemaneh26_1]. The IPCC figure is a count of people who could benefit, not a measured effect [ev_food_security_ipccsrccl6_6]. The food-access review included only studies showing improvement in at least one food-security dimension, so its finding says nothing about studies that found no benefit, and one of its cited studies is a life-cycle assessment rather than a population survey [ev_food_security_nguy24n_1]. The Kenyan flood-fruit finding is farmer-reported [ev_food_security_thorlak12_1].

All units sit in low, lower-middle and LIC/LMIC-pooled African and Timorese contexts, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9, ev_food_security_seghieri19_13, ev_food_security_talensi21_3].

justification.mechanism: Across regeneration-based farmland (FMNR), several sources find fewer households going hungry. A World Vision meta-brief across seven African and one Timorese project catchments found project participants reported significantly fewer months of food shortage, by 0.26 months, than non-participants [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9]. In Senegal, only 3% of FMNR adopters failed to meet annual food needs for more than 4 months in one zone, against 14% of non-adopters, and 0% versus 4% in another zone [ev_food_security_seghieri19_13]. In the Sahel, moving from low-intensity to young-level FMNR raised the household food consumption score by about 12% [ev_food_security_bina15_7]. In Ghana's Talensi project, households with sufficient diet diversity rose from 44.5% at baseline to 55.8% at endline, and households with one or more hungry months in the previous year fell from 68.2% to 41%, though this project bundled FMNR with savings groups, post-harvest storage and value-chain and livestock work, so the gain is not attributable to FMNR alone [ev_food_security_talensi21_3, ev_food_security_talensi21_4]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates food security and self-sufficiency improved, reasoning that more diversified livelihoods reduce the risk of food insecurity [ev_food_security_wocat_507_2019_food_security_selfsufficiency].
justification.conditionality: The class stays slight rather than higher because some units find no effect: in Niger, FMNR does not appear to reduce the number of months of perceived food shortage, though it does seem to raise crop diversity, and in the Sahel the number of months with a household food deficit showed no significant effect for any FMNR intensity, with resilience during shortages read by the authors as an inference rather than a measured result [ev_food_security_haglund11_1, ev_food_security_bina15_9]. The Sahel food-consumption-score gain from low to continuous FMNR was also not significant [ev_food_security_bina15_8]. The Talensi gains are a World Vision self-evaluation, before-and-after with no control group and an acknowledged change in sampling, and the project itself attributes part of the hungry-months improvement to better food storage rather than FMNR [ev_food_security_talensi21_3, ev_food_security_talensi21_4]; the World Vision multi-country figure likewise notes the FMNR effect cannot be fully disentangled from other project activities [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9]. The WOCAT rating is a compiler's assessment on a technology sheet, not a measurement [ev_food_security_wocat_507_2019_food_security_selfsufficiency]. All units sit in low, lower-middle and LIC/LMIC-pooled African and Timorese contexts, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_food_security_wvfmnr19_9, ev_food_security_seghieri19_13, ev_food_security_talensi21_3].

effect_mechanism: A gender review finds agroforestry can offer substantial benefits to women, but their participation is low in enterprises considered men's domain such as timber and in the area and number of trees they commit [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_1]. It reports, second-hand, that management labour often falls on women (in 89% of Embu households using calliandra fodder, females managed it) [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2], that 32% of males and 23% of females planted improved fallows in four Zambian villages [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3], and that in farmer-managed trials women had somewhat higher Sesbania survival than men [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4].
conditionality: The evidence is too thin to state a class: every unit comes from a single narrative review of sub-Saharan African studies, read second-hand, with no measured finding of its own [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_1, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4]. A further independent source or a measured change in inequity is what is missing. The cited figures point both ways (labour and uptake gaps against women, a trial advantage for women) and are shares of households or participants, not changes caused by agroforestry [ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_2, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_3, ev_gender_inequity_kiptot11_4].

effect_mechanism: Trees cool the air and soil that crops and livestock experience, through shade and altered radiation and humidity. In Ethiopia, air temperature at wheat floral height was lowered by up to 6°C at midday under Faidherbia albida canopy compared with the open field, reaching a maximum of 29°C under the canopy against 36°C in the open, and temperature stayed above 28°C for about six hours a day in the open field against under two hours under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1]. In Germany, poplar alley cropping measured 3.4°C lower air temperature than sole wheat on hot summer days [ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found summer air temperature significantly reduced by 4.01% compared with unsheltered farmland [ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. In Sahelian parklands, trees reduce the maximum daily temperature by an average of 1 to 2.5°C, with stronger effects on hotter, drier days, and under Acacia tortilis canopy in Senegal's Ferlo, air temperatures ranged from 29 to 36°C against 26 to 42°C outside the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. In cocoa agroforestry across ten countries, the canopy of shade trees keeps mean temperature lower and buffers daily maximum and minimum temperatures compared with monoculture [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. For livestock, the cooling under trees is reported to reduce heat stress directly: temperature under tree crowns in tropical pastures is 2 to 9°C lower than in open areas, with tree groups giving the largest reduction (3.6°C) and live fences the smallest (1.7°C) [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. In Brazil's Caatinga, the black-globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 to 84.2 and radiant thermal load also fell comparing shade under tree strips with sun exposure, and strips with the most woody cover were more efficient at mitigating cattle heat load than an almost treeless system, with the cooling effect holding even when the trees were leafless in the dry season [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]. In Brazilian silvopasture compared with monoculture pasture, the area reaching critical thermal-comfort levels for animals fell by 20 to 100% [ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. A Peru/Colombia systematic review reports silvopastoral systems reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13°C on the hottest days [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1]. The IPCC AR6 AFOLU chapter states in the same terms that agroforestry reduces ambient temperatures and crop heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6_1].
conditionality: Against this, one measured unit in Senegal finds windbreak hedges generally cause a slight rise in temperature in the protected plots rather than cooling them, with variable impacts depending on crop and growth stage — the practice worsening the outcome for some adopters, which the engine counts as measured harm [ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_16]. The IPCC AR6 WG2 chapter adds that while shade trees can ameliorate rising stand temperatures for arabica coffee, the opposite can also be true [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2]. In Ghana, cocoa shade trees were confirmed to moderate the microclimate especially during dry and extremely dry periods, but daily mean maximum air temperatures still reached up to 44°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3]. A Brazilian systematic review of silvopastoral thermal-comfort studies found most studies showed no significant difference in the temperature-humidity index between silvopastoral and treeless pasture, which the authors partly attribute to the index ignoring solar radiation — the main pathway through which trees reduce heat load [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. In Mexican coffee, seasonal mean temperature (as opposed to day-to-day fluctuation) was not significantly different along a shade gradient [ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_2]. No unit in this row measures a severe or extreme heat event, only ordinary hot-season or hot-day conditions [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1]. The pooled evidence spans many countries across West Africa, East Africa, Latin America, South and East Asia, temperate Europe and Australia/the USA at every income level, so it transfers only as adjacent rather than squarely in context [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_dobhal24_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_hao26_1].

effect_mechanism: Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the dry Colombian Caribbean, silvopastoral models most intensive in shrubs, trees and rotational pasture reduce heat stress in cattle [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1]. In Cuba live fences came to be used to shade cattle and avoid stress, and Neotropical livestock keepers value shade because it reduces heat stress and supports reproduction, weight gain and milk production [ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_3, ev_microclimate_buffering_moran18_8]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. conditionality: Not every heat measure moved: in the same review, results for the temperature humidity index were unclear, with four of the seven studies that used it finding no significant difference from treeless pasture; the authors attribute this partly to that index leaving out solar radiation, the main pathway through which trees cut heat load [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. effect_mechanism: Faidherbia albida parkland trees on Ethiopian wheat farms lowered midday air temperature by up to 6°C, peaking at 29 °C under the canopy against 36 °C in the open field, and in Senegal's Ferlo air temperatures under Acacia tortilis ranged between 29 °C and 36 °C against 26 °C to 42 °C outside the cover [ev_microclimate_buffering_sida18_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_faosen24_6]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, maximum daily temperature fell by an average of 1–2.5 °C and minimum air humidity rose by up to 5%, with stronger differences on hotter and drier days [ev_microclimate_buffering_bayala14_2].
