effect_mechanism: Shade trees in coffee and cocoa systems cool the canopy microclimate. A cocoa meta-analysis across ten countries found the canopy of shade trees keeps mean temperature lower and buffers daily maximum and minimum temperatures compared with monoculture, with potential to reduce the impact of rising mean temperatures and temperature extremes [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1]. In Ghana, shade trees were confirmed to moderate the microclimate especially during dry and extremely dry periods, though daily mean maximum air temperatures still reached up to 44°C [ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3]. In Costa Rica, shade reduces the maximum air temperature by 1.7°C and buffers air and soil temperature, reduces wind speed, and raises relative humidity and soil moisture under the canopy [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_9]. A review synthesis states shade trees reduce canopy temperatures by 2 to 4°C, mitigating heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4], and in Central America shade trees are reported to have improved microclimate stability [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_7]. Across a multi-country tropical review, trees under canopies averaging 20 m tall gave a temperature reduction of about 2°C compared with a treeless site [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2]. In Mexican coffee along a shade gradient, the high-shade site fluctuated least around the crop's optimum temperature of 20°C, staying closer to it than medium- and low-shade sites [ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_1]. The IPCC AR6 WG2 chapter states shade trees can ameliorate increasing stand temperatures that would significantly affect arabica coffee [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2].
conditionality: The same IPCC chapter immediately adds that the opposite can also be true, pointing to the drought-season soil-water competition recorded in the Ghanaian cocoa study above [ev_microclimate_buffering_ipccar6ch5_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_abdul18_3]. The same Patil review that found shade stabilising microclimate in Central America also reports that excessive shading combined with heavy rain raised the risk of fungal infection in parts of East Africa [ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_7]. For seasonal mean temperature rather than day-to-day fluctuation, the Mexican coffee sites were not significantly different along the shade gradient, which the author reads as shade changing fluctuations more than seasonal means [ev_microclimate_buffering_lin07_2]. None of the ten units states a size for the gain beyond temperature differences of 1.7 to 4°C; none measures a severe or extreme heat event, only ordinary hot days or dry seasons [ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_patil25_4]. The evidence spans lower-middle, upper-middle, mostly-upper-middle and high-income cocoa and coffee countries across West and Central Africa, Southeast Asia and Latin America, so it transfers only as adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_microclimate_buffering_niether20_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_seghieri19_4].

effect_mechanism: In the dry Colombian Caribbean, silvopastoral models most intensive in shrubs, trees and rotational pasture reduce heat stress in cattle, and a Brazilian study found agroforestry reduced the area at critical thermal-comfort levels for animals by 20 to 100% compared with monoculture pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. In tropical silvopasture, temperatures under tree crowns can average 2-5°C lower than outside them throughout the year, depending on the characteristics of the trees [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1]. Under tree crowns, temperature reductions of 2 to 9 °C relative to open areas have been reported, and in Cañas, Costa Rica, temperatures in the hottest hours were 3.6 °C, 2.9 °C and 1.7 °C lower under tree groups, single trees and live fences respectively than in open pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. Silvopastoral systems can reduce paddock air temperature by up to 13 °C on the hottest days, and trees in paddocks shade animals against excessive solar radiation, reducing heat stress [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. In the semi-arid Caatinga of Brazil, the black globe temperature-humidity index fell from 89.2 in the sun to 84.2 in the shade of native tree strips at 10 am and 2 pm, the strips kept radiant thermal load and the index lower even when leafless in the dormant season, and a cited study found the silvopasture with more woody cover mitigated cattle heat load better [ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_3]. A systematic review of silvopasture and dairy cattle, mostly from Brazil, found the effect on the thermal environment was mostly (57%) favourable: silvopasture gave lower air temperature, black globe temperature, soil surface temperature and radiant thermal load than treeless pasture, and cows drank less often and had lower surface temperature and respiratory rate [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_1]. An older review cites Kelly et al. (1950) that trees are the most effective shade for cattle, adding evaporative cooling from the leaves to protection from sunlight [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].
conditionality: The Colombian and Brazilian review results are cited secondary findings from upper-middle-income settings, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target [ev_microclimate_buffering_murg13_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santos25_10]. Most of the Latin American units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews, while the Brazilian Caatinga preprint measured the thermal indices itself [ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_santosneto22_2]; the 13 °C figure is an upper value for the hottest days, and the Costa Rican units are high-income evidence [ev_microclimate_buffering_saucedo23_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_navas10_2]. All units report air temperature, thermal indices or animal comfort, components of heat-stress impact rather than measured losses [ev_microclimate_buffering_montagnini15_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_cisneros24_1]. Not every index moves: in the same systematic review, results for the temperature humidity index, which uses only air temperature and humidity, were unclear, with most of the studies that used it finding no significant difference between silvopasture and treeless pasture [ev_microclimate_buffering_deniz23_2]. The cattle-shade statement from Australia and the USA is an old citation without a tree system [ev_microclimate_buffering_blackshaw94_1].

effect_mechanism: The production evidence splits by sub-practice. Regeneration-based farmland, planted silvoarable systems and the cross-family syntheses each lean to a strong gain on their own, while silvopastoral, boundary and shaded perennial (coffee and cocoa) systems record both gains and losses. Meta-analyses report higher crop yield under agroforestry than controls in sub-Saharan Africa and higher soil nitrogen stocks than crop monocultures in the humid tropics, with soil nitrogen used here as a component of the production gap [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. A meta-analysis cited in Arslan et al. (Branca et al.) associates agroforestry techniques with a 69% increase in cereal yields across the studies it consulted [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. In the Sahel, millet yields are reported to double or triple under Faidherbia albida and yields were higher where intensive FMNR is practised, and tree shade in pastures is associated with gains in milk production and weight gain [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_14, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded 23-26% more grain than open-field wheat in the normal seasons of 2013 and 2014, and up to 85% more in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low; available N close to the crowns was 35-55% larger than under sole wheat [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_1]. Lower yield variability under more diverse shade is cited as a sign of greater yield resistance to shocks in shaded systems, and Kenyan agroforestry-project farmers in Lower Nyando raised farm productivity against a control group [ev_crop_yield_morel24_4, ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Fertilizer trees raise maize output: in Malawi, adopters had a 35% higher value of food crop production and 32% higher maize productivity than their counterfactual, and a review notes fertilizer tree species are widely documented to substantially increase maize yields compared with maize grown without fertilizer in Zambia and across Africa [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_lasco14_1]. In maize–Gliricidia trials run for 12-13 consecutive years in Malawi and Zambia, the intercrop gave the most stable yield at Makoka and more stable yields than fertilized maize at Msekera, and the intercrop with 50% of the recommended N and P fertilizer matched the yield of fully fertilized monoculture maize [ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_2]. Maize yields were more stable with Leucaena hedgerows than in monocrop, as also shown for alley cropping and fertilizer trees [ev_yield_stability_lasco14_1]. In Maradi, Niger, millet yields rose by 120 to 209 kg/ha where FMNR was older than 6 years, with smaller increases for younger FMNR, and FMNR is estimated to have raised yields by an average of 100 kg/ha over 5 million hectares [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3]. In Lempira, Honduras, an ICRAF working paper reports that the Quesungual system raised maize yields from 1.9 to 3.2 tonnes per hectare and bean yields from 0.8 to 2.0 tonnes per hectare [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_2]. In Lempira, Honduras, farmers are reporting maize yield increases of a minimum of 60% after moving from slash-and-burn to the Quesungual system, and fields under continuous maize for seven years on 35% slopes and poor soil average 2.9 t/ha, against a best of 1.6 t/ha on the same fields before [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, tuber yield is improved (+0.40 to +1.67 t ha-1) and legumes are less affected than cereals, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. In subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. In Colombian intensive silvopasture, milk production was 32.1% higher than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture raises stocking rates up to four times above extensive grazing and with them meat and milk output per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1]. In Colombia, a Leucaena-based silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows ha-1 while eliminating chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During El Niño events, milk production fell by 2.2% in silvopastoral systems against 4.9% in conventional systems [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture compared with full sun, and dry-season weight gains were 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. In shaded coffee and cocoa, a coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss (OR = 0.69) and a cocoa meta-analysis found total system yields about ten times higher than in monocultures [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_2]. Planted legume trees in maize systems hold up in synthesis: a meta-analysis of studies from West, East and southern Africa put the maize yield response ratio at 1.27–1.43 after rotational improved fallows of non-coppicing woody legumes and 1.11–1.30 with relay intercrops, against unfertilised maize, and the yield increase was 1.6 t ha−1 with coppicing woody legumes [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_3]. In the forest zone of Cameroon, maize grain yield in Leucaena alley plots rose from the first to the third year while yield in the treeless control fell, and groundnut in the alleys also out-yielded the control [ev_crop_yield_tonye95_1, ev_crop_yield_tonye95_2]. At Sadore, Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised sole millet yields by 41 % in the unfertilised control and by 10 % with farmyard manure, raised crop income by 5 to 14 % without counting the fruit, and from 2 to 3 times once fruit sales were included [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1, ev_crop_yield_bado21_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_2]. In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii intercropped in smallholder coffee and returned as mulch raised coffee yields by 400 kg ha−1, a 23–36% increase over the farmer's mulch practice across the two seasons [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1]. Among sub-Saharan adoption studies, high-quality maize studies show a significant gain for adopters (Cohen's d = 0.27, 95% CI: 0.12 to 0.42) [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]; a pest-control meta-analysis notes that the studies testing whether agroforestry pest control translated into crop yield both found it did [ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]; and a hedgerow meta-analysis found plant hedgerows raised soil total N (SMD = 1.33; 95% CI 0.98–1.68) [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. More recent additions to this evidence pool mostly repeat the same pattern. In Kenya, improved-fallow soil-fertility trials raised maize yield by a mean of 128% against no-input plots (median 167%), close to the 114% mean for biomass transfer and above the 89% mean for mineral fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_place05_1]. A pan-tropical meta-analysis found soil available nitrogen 46% higher under agroforestry than crop monocultures, with a mean response ratio of 1.46 [ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_2]. In Brazil, cassava under tree cover yielded up to 101.99 kg/ha against zero for the unshaded monoculture control in one season [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1], and a review of coconut-based systems in Sri Lanka reports increased nut yields when pasture grasses, black pepper and coffee are intercropped with coconut [ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1].
conditionality: The sub-practices disagree, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence rather than a strong gain. On the gain side, regeneration-based farmland (Faidherbia albida and Piliostigma reticulatum parklands, FMNR in Niger and Ghana, the Quesungual system) and the cross-family meta-analyses and assessments show higher yields or soil nitrogen [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_15, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. On the conflicting side, shaded perennial systems pair those system-level gains with main-crop losses: cocoa yields 25% lower than in monocultures, coffee and cocoa yield per hectare 26% lower than conventional systems, and coffee yields declining under >60% shade, while shade did not prevent the drought-induced cocoa yield decline in a Ghanaian experiment [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the separator there is whether the by-crops are counted and how dense the shade is, and the units are crop-specific to coffee, cocoa and coconut. Planted silvoarable systems now lean to a gain, but still record tree–crop competition losses next to the fertilizer-tree and Gliricidia gains; silvopasture pairs Latin American milk and stocking gains with a global review's losses under dispersed trees; and boundary planting pairs higher yields within sheltered farmland with losses at shelterbelt edges and in windbreak paddocks [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The separator, in the sources' own terms, is spacing, tree density, tree age and distance from the tree line: alley spacings under 10 TH were predicted to reduce yields, pasture yield fell as tree density rose and under the oldest trees, livestock yield fell with more trees and older trees, and yield losses were reported up to 10 m from hedges in the rainy season and in shelterbelt edge zones [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_16, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The evidence pulls both ways: tree–crop competition for water delayed Kenyan maize and could cause crop failure, intercropped wheat in China and soybean in Brazil yielded less than monocultures, groundnut and millet yields fell under Cordyla pinnata in Senegal, and excess shade can reduce pasture productivity [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_5, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11, ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. The pooled magnitude combines a crop-yield response ratio with a soil-nitrogen response ratio, and a systematic review's pooled crop-yield effect across agroforestry interventions had a confidence interval spanning zero [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_1]. The Lower Nyando productivity gain had large standard errors and was not significant, and the yield-variability finding is a cited statement [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. Gains are not universal: Malawian non-adopters would have lost food crop value had they adopted fertilizer trees, at Msekera fertilized monoculture maize out-yielded the maize–Gliricidia intercrop, and some stability models there ranked unfertilized control maize as more stable than the intercrop [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_3]. The Malawi estimates come from an ICRAF working paper evaluating an ICRAF-promoted technology, and the Gliricidia trials compare against fertilized maize rather than farmer practice [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1]. Cereals often lose: in Maradi, FMNR did not significantly increase grain yields, the income gain being attributed to crop diversification instead, and under parkland trees cereal grain yield ranged from a loss of 0.54 t ha-1 under Balanites aegyptiaca to a gain of 0.24 t ha-1 under F. albida, with reductions attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water [ev_crop_yield_haglund11_1, ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. The Niger yield figures are earlier estimates cited in a grey-literature review, and the Honduran yields are before-and-after case-study figures for a slash-and-mulch system [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1]. Next to the trees the effect reverses: crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields lined with old field shelterbelts, cereal yields next to the belt were depressed out to about 10 m from the field edge in all 3 years, a competition effect; the sheltered zone beyond it gave above-average yields in 1989 and 1990, but in 1991, a season with well above average water availability, that beneficial zone was absent [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. Taking the mid-field yield as the reference, the authors estimate a net field yield loss equal to the width of the shelterbelt, though they doubt that mid-field is the right baseline [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt study is measured, but it is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; its net loss is measured against the mid-field yield rather than an unsheltered field, a baseline the authors themselves question [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. In the West African Sahel, live fences and fodder banks reduced yields in the first year, which recovered in the second [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Tree density matters: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. The Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Costa Rican livestock units are high-income evidence [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. A global quantitative review against treeless controls found average losses for windbreaks, alleys and dispersed trees: windbreak paddocks −8.3%, alleys −17.63%, pasture under dispersed trees −20.8% and livestock there −18.6%, with gains only at wide spacings (+13% at 15 tree heights between alleys, +8.04% across a windbreak paddock 20 tree heights wide) [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. The cited 69% cereal-yield figure reaches this row second-hand through Arslan et al.: the citing text does not describe the agroforestry techniques further and reports no significance [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. Of the newer primary studies, regeneration-based farmland again holds the stronger result: The Ethiopian drought-year gain stays separate from the normal-season gain; at the same site soil total N did not differ significantly under and outside the canopy at the end of the 2013 season despite the larger available N near the crowns, and the yield benefit of canopy cooling is modelled and appeared only with applied N [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_2, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. The Ontario windbreak gain is high-income boreal evidence from a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site, with plots irrigated from ditches, so it does not test competition next to the trees [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. In southern Malawi a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop, which produces leafy residues but no grain, gave the same quantity of maize grain as monoculture maize fertilised in the same way, so no yield gain [ev_crop_yield_snapp10_1]. The newer evidence repeats these splits. Across sub-Saharan adoption studies agroforestry is not associated with a statistically significant effect on yield overall (Cohen's d = 0.35, 95% CI: −0.07 to 0.78, p = 0.14), the gain appearing only in the high-quality maize subset, and the review notes many adoption studies have weak causal identification [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1, ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]. At Sadore the Ziziphus gain depended on the fertiliser: millet yield fell by 13 % under the trees with NPK, intercropped millet fell by 4 and 11 % with NPK alone and with NPK and manure, and cowpea fell by 15 % in the unfertilised control, probably from tree shade, though it rose 9% with NPK [ev_crop_yield_bado21_3, ev_crop_yield_bado21_7, ev_crop_yield_bado21_4, ev_crop_yield_bado21_5, ev_crop_yield_bado21_6]; soil N there did not differ significantly with and without the trees, and tree presence was neither randomised nor replicated across the two blocks [ev_soil_nitrogen_bado21_1]. Young fruit trees compete hard: between juvenile plumcot rows in irrigated semi-arid Xinjiang, China (upper-middle income), soybean yield fell by 46.03% and alfalfa by 51.83% against sole crops, partly because the intercrop had a smaller cropped area and lower seeding rate [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In the Rwandan coffee trial the Tephrosia gain was significant only in the first season [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_2], and a review of dairy silvopasture found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. The Sileshi maize meta-analysis compares against unfertilised maize, not farmer practice with fertiliser, and its authors note signs of publication bias [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1]; the hedgerow meta-analysis mixes grass-only strips with woody hedgerows [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. The Honduran yield figures are farmer reports relayed by the project's promoters in a grey-literature article and a before-and-after comparison with the best earlier yield, not a concurrent control; the gain belongs to the bundle of trees, mulch, zero tillage and no burning, not to the trees alone [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6]. Among the units added since the last round, several further losses and reversals appear. A global quantitative review found no significant difference in yield across three yield types (crop, crop biomass, pasture) sheltered by trees, with crop yield down 9.2% and crop biomass down 9.3% on average, and only pasture yield showing a small average increase (+3.1%) [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_2, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_3]. In Costa Rica, coffee under Erythrina shade of 40-60% cover produced 41% fewer fruits per tree than coffee under a maximum of 20% shade cover (1091 against 1838 fruits) [ev_crop_yield_villa20_1], and a further Costa Rican shade-coffee comparison found a 30% yield reduction under agroforestry against monoculture [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. In Bolivia, cocoa productivity was on average 41% higher in monoculture than in agroforestry, though the authors note agroforestry revenues economically compensate for the difference [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6]. In Cameroon, cocoa yields above 1.5 t/ha are not compatible with carbon storage (shade) above 100-150 t C/ha, and storage above that level caps accessible yield at about 750 kg/ha [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6]. A standardised-mean-difference review finds effect sizes ranging from −0.33 for a payments-for-ecosystem-services programme in Nicaragua to 3.85 for improved fallows raising crop value in Malawi — an enormous spread within one review — and, in a certification-scheme comparison, Organic and Utz coffee certification were associated with statistically significant yield reductions (Hedges' g −0.488 and −0.465) while three other certification schemes showed insignificant increases [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_2, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_3, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_4]. In Senegal, groundnut response under parkland tree canopy is reported variable with no consistent direction across studies, and windbreak hedges are reported to have a neutral effect on groundnut yield at Bambey [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_10, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_14].

justification.mechanism: The production evidence splits by sub-practice. Regeneration-based farmland, planted silvoarable systems and the cross-family syntheses each lean to a strong gain on their own, while silvopastoral, boundary and shaded perennial (coffee and cocoa) systems record both gains and losses. Meta-analyses report higher crop yield under agroforestry than controls in sub-Saharan Africa and higher soil nitrogen stocks than crop monocultures in the humid tropics, with soil nitrogen used here as a component of the production gap [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. A meta-analysis cited in Arslan et al. (Branca et al.) associates agroforestry techniques with a 69% increase in cereal yields across the studies it consulted [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. In the Sahel, millet yields are reported to double or triple under Faidherbia albida and yields were higher where intensive FMNR is practised, and tree shade in pastures is associated with gains in milk production and weight gain [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_14, ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]. On paired on-farm plots in Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded 23-26% more grain than open-field wheat in the normal seasons of 2013 and 2014, and up to 85% more in 2015, an El Niño year in which both yields were low; available N close to the crowns was 35-55% larger than under sole wheat [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_1]. Lower yield variability under more diverse shade is cited as a sign of greater yield resistance to shocks in shaded systems, and Kenyan agroforestry-project farmers in Lower Nyando raised farm productivity against a control group [ev_crop_yield_morel24_4, ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Fertilizer trees raise maize output: in Malawi, adopters had a 35% higher value of food crop production and 32% higher maize productivity than their counterfactual, and a review notes fertilizer tree species are widely documented to substantially increase maize yields compared with maize grown without fertilizer in Zambia and across Africa [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_lasco14_1]. In maize–Gliricidia trials run for 12-13 consecutive years in Malawi and Zambia, the intercrop gave the most stable yield at Makoka and more stable yields than fertilized maize at Msekera, and the intercrop with 50% of the recommended N and P fertilizer matched the yield of fully fertilized monoculture maize [ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_2]. Maize yields were more stable with Leucaena hedgerows than in monocrop, as also shown for alley cropping and fertilizer trees [ev_yield_stability_lasco14_1]. In Maradi, Niger, millet yields rose by 120 to 209 kg/ha where FMNR was older than 6 years, with smaller increases for younger FMNR, and FMNR is estimated to have raised yields by an average of 100 kg/ha over 5 million hectares [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3]. In Lempira, Honduras, an ICRAF working paper reports that the Quesungual system raised maize yields from 1.9 to 3.2 tonnes per hectare and bean yields from 0.8 to 2.0 tonnes per hectare [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_2]. In Lempira, Honduras, farmers are reporting maize yield increases of a minimum of 60% after moving from slash-and-burn to the Quesungual system, and fields under continuous maize for seven years on 35% slopes and poor soil average 2.9 t/ha, against a best of 1.6 t/ha on the same fields before [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6]. Under Sahelian parkland trees, tuber yield is improved (+0.40 to +1.67 t ha-1) and legumes are less affected than cereals, and tree fodder is crucial in the dry season and during drought [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1, ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1]. A meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. In subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. In Colombian intensive silvopasture, milk production was 32.1% higher than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture raises stocking rates up to four times above extensive grazing and with them meat and milk output per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1]. In Colombia, a Leucaena-based silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows ha-1 while eliminating chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During El Niño events, milk production fell by 2.2% in silvopastoral systems against 4.9% in conventional systems [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture compared with full sun, and dry-season weight gains were 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. In shaded coffee and cocoa, a coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss (OR = 0.69) and a cocoa meta-analysis found total system yields about ten times higher than in monocultures [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_2]. Planted legume trees in maize systems hold up in synthesis: a meta-analysis of studies from West, East and southern Africa put the maize yield response ratio at 1.27–1.43 after rotational improved fallows of non-coppicing woody legumes and 1.11–1.30 with relay intercrops, against unfertilised maize, and the yield increase was 1.6 t ha−1 with coppicing woody legumes [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_3]. In the forest zone of Cameroon, maize grain yield in Leucaena alley plots rose from the first to the third year while yield in the treeless control fell, and groundnut in the alleys also out-yielded the control [ev_crop_yield_tonye95_1, ev_crop_yield_tonye95_2]. At Sadore, Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised sole millet yields by 41 % in the unfertilised control and by 10 % with farmyard manure, raised crop income by 5 to 14 % without counting the fruit, and from 2 to 3 times once fruit sales were included [ev_crop_yield_bado21_1, ev_crop_yield_bado21_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_1, ev_agricultural_production_value_bado21_2]. In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii intercropped in smallholder coffee and returned as mulch raised coffee yields by 400 kg ha−1, a 23–36% increase over the farmer's mulch practice across the two seasons [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1]. Among sub-Saharan adoption studies, high-quality maize studies show a significant gain for adopters (Cohen's d = 0.27, 95% CI: 0.12 to 0.42) [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]; a pest-control meta-analysis notes that the studies testing whether agroforestry pest control translated into crop yield both found it did [ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]; and a hedgerow meta-analysis found plant hedgerows raised soil total N (SMD = 1.33; 95% CI 0.98–1.68) [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. More recent additions to this evidence pool mostly repeat the same pattern. In Kenya, improved-fallow soil-fertility trials raised maize yield by a mean of 128% against no-input plots (median 167%), close to the 114% mean for biomass transfer and above the 89% mean for mineral fertiliser [ev_crop_yield_place05_1]. A pan-tropical meta-analysis found soil available nitrogen 46% higher under agroforestry than crop monocultures, with a mean response ratio of 1.46 [ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_2]. In Brazil, cassava under tree cover yielded up to 101.99 kg/ha against zero for the unshaded monoculture control in one season [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1], and a review of coconut-based systems in Sri Lanka reports increased nut yields when pasture grasses, black pepper and coffee are intercropped with coconut [ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1].
justification.conditionality: The sub-practices disagree, so the roll-up states conflicting evidence rather than a strong gain. On the gain side, regeneration-based farmland (Faidherbia albida and Piliostigma reticulatum parklands, FMNR in Niger and Ghana, the Quesungual system) and the cross-family meta-analyses and assessments show higher yields or soil nitrogen [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_15, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6, ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. On the conflicting side, shaded perennial systems pair those system-level gains with main-crop losses: cocoa yields 25% lower than in monocultures, coffee and cocoa yield per hectare 26% lower than conventional systems, and coffee yields declining under >60% shade, while shade did not prevent the drought-induced cocoa yield decline in a Ghanaian experiment [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2]; the separator there is whether the by-crops are counted and how dense the shade is, and the units are crop-specific to coffee, cocoa and coconut. Planted silvoarable systems now lean to a gain, but still record tree–crop competition losses next to the fertilizer-tree and Gliricidia gains; silvopasture pairs Latin American milk and stocking gains with a global review's losses under dispersed trees; and boundary planting pairs higher yields within sheltered farmland with losses at shelterbelt edges and in windbreak paddocks [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_2, ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The separator, in the sources' own terms, is spacing, tree density, tree age and distance from the tree line: alley spacings under 10 TH were predicted to reduce yields, pasture yield fell as tree density rose and under the oldest trees, livestock yield fell with more trees and older trees, and yield losses were reported up to 10 m from hedges in the rainy season and in shelterbelt edge zones [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_7, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_16, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The evidence pulls both ways: tree–crop competition for water delayed Kenyan maize and could cause crop failure, intercropped wheat in China and soybean in Brazil yielded less than monocultures, groundnut and millet yields fell under Cordyla pinnata in Senegal, and excess shade can reduce pasture productivity [ev_crop_yield_watts22_10, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_santos25_5, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11, ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. The pooled magnitude combines a crop-yield response ratio with a soil-nitrogen response ratio, and a systematic review's pooled crop-yield effect across agroforestry interventions had a confidence interval spanning zero [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_1]. The Lower Nyando productivity gain had large standard errors and was not significant, and the yield-variability finding is a cited statement [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4]. Gains are not universal: Malawian non-adopters would have lost food crop value had they adopted fertilizer trees, at Msekera fertilized monoculture maize out-yielded the maize–Gliricidia intercrop, and some stability models there ranked unfertilized control maize as more stable than the intercrop [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_2, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1, ev_yield_stability_sileshi12_3]. The Malawi estimates come from an ICRAF working paper evaluating an ICRAF-promoted technology, and the Gliricidia trials compare against fertilized maize rather than farmer practice [ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_sileshi12_1]. Cereals often lose: in Maradi, FMNR did not significantly increase grain yields, the income gain being attributed to crop diversification instead, and under parkland trees cereal grain yield ranged from a loss of 0.54 t ha-1 under Balanites aegyptiaca to a gain of 0.24 t ha-1 under F. albida, with reductions attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water [ev_crop_yield_haglund11_1, ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. The Niger yield figures are earlier estimates cited in a grey-literature review, and the Honduran yields are before-and-after case-study figures for a slash-and-mulch system [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1]. Next to the trees the effect reverses: crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields lined with old field shelterbelts, cereal yields next to the belt were depressed out to about 10 m from the field edge in all 3 years, a competition effect; the sheltered zone beyond it gave above-average yields in 1989 and 1990, but in 1991, a season with well above average water availability, that beneficial zone was absent [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. Taking the mid-field yield as the reference, the authors estimate a net field yield loss equal to the width of the shelterbelt, though they doubt that mid-field is the right baseline [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt study is measured, but it is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; its net loss is measured against the mid-field yield rather than an unsheltered field, a baseline the authors themselves question [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. In the West African Sahel, live fences and fodder banks reduced yields in the first year, which recovered in the second [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Tree density matters: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. The Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. The Costa Rican livestock units are high-income evidence [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. A global quantitative review against treeless controls found average losses for windbreaks, alleys and dispersed trees: windbreak paddocks −8.3%, alleys −17.63%, pasture under dispersed trees −20.8% and livestock there −18.6%, with gains only at wide spacings (+13% at 15 tree heights between alleys, +8.04% across a windbreak paddock 20 tree heights wide) [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_6, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_8, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. The cited 69% cereal-yield figure reaches this row second-hand through Arslan et al.: the citing text does not describe the agroforestry techniques further and reports no significance [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. Of the newer primary studies, regeneration-based farmland again holds the stronger result: The Ethiopian drought-year gain stays separate from the normal-season gain; at the same site soil total N did not differ significantly under and outside the canopy at the end of the 2013 season despite the larger available N near the crowns, and the yield benefit of canopy cooling is modelled and appeared only with applied N [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_2, ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4]. The Ontario windbreak gain is high-income boreal evidence from a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site, with plots irrigated from ditches, so it does not test competition next to the trees [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. In southern Malawi a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop, which produces leafy residues but no grain, gave the same quantity of maize grain as monoculture maize fertilised in the same way, so no yield gain [ev_crop_yield_snapp10_1]. The newer evidence repeats these splits. Across sub-Saharan adoption studies agroforestry is not associated with a statistically significant effect on yield overall (Cohen's d = 0.35, 95% CI: −0.07 to 0.78, p = 0.14), the gain appearing only in the high-quality maize subset, and the review notes many adoption studies have weak causal identification [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1, ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]. At Sadore the Ziziphus gain depended on the fertiliser: millet yield fell by 13 % under the trees with NPK, intercropped millet fell by 4 and 11 % with NPK alone and with NPK and manure, and cowpea fell by 15 % in the unfertilised control, probably from tree shade, though it rose 9% with NPK [ev_crop_yield_bado21_3, ev_crop_yield_bado21_7, ev_crop_yield_bado21_4, ev_crop_yield_bado21_5, ev_crop_yield_bado21_6]; soil N there did not differ significantly with and without the trees, and tree presence was neither randomised nor replicated across the two blocks [ev_soil_nitrogen_bado21_1]. Young fruit trees compete hard: between juvenile plumcot rows in irrigated semi-arid Xinjiang, China (upper-middle income), soybean yield fell by 46.03% and alfalfa by 51.83% against sole crops, partly because the intercrop had a smaller cropped area and lower seeding rate [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In the Rwandan coffee trial the Tephrosia gain was significant only in the first season [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_2], and a review of dairy silvopasture found no significant difference in milk production in the studies that measured it [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. The Sileshi maize meta-analysis compares against unfertilised maize, not farmer practice with fertiliser, and its authors note signs of publication bias [ev_crop_yield_sileshi08_1]; the hedgerow meta-analysis mixes grass-only strips with woody hedgerows [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. The Honduran yield figures are farmer reports relayed by the project's promoters in a grey-literature article and a before-and-after comparison with the best earlier yield, not a concurrent control; the gain belongs to the bundle of trees, mulch, zero tillage and no burning, not to the trees alone [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6]. Among the units added since the last round, several further losses and reversals appear. A global quantitative review found no significant difference in yield across three yield types (crop, crop biomass, pasture) sheltered by trees, with crop yield down 9.2% and crop biomass down 9.3% on average, and only pasture yield showing a small average increase (+3.1%) [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_2, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_3]. In Costa Rica, coffee under Erythrina shade of 40-60% cover produced 41% fewer fruits per tree than coffee under a maximum of 20% shade cover (1091 against 1838 fruits) [ev_crop_yield_villa20_1], and a further Costa Rican shade-coffee comparison found a 30% yield reduction under agroforestry against monoculture [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. In Bolivia, cocoa productivity was on average 41% higher in monoculture than in agroforestry, though the authors note agroforestry revenues economically compensate for the difference [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6]. In Cameroon, cocoa yields above 1.5 t/ha are not compatible with carbon storage (shade) above 100-150 t C/ha, and storage above that level caps accessible yield at about 750 kg/ha [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6]. A standardised-mean-difference review finds effect sizes ranging from −0.33 for a payments-for-ecosystem-services programme in Nicaragua to 3.85 for improved fallows raising crop value in Malawi — an enormous spread within one review — and, in a certification-scheme comparison, Organic and Utz coffee certification were associated with statistically significant yield reductions (Hedges' g −0.488 and −0.465) while three other certification schemes showed insignificant increases [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_2, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_3, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_4]. In Senegal, groundnut response under parkland tree canopy is reported variable with no consistent direction across studies, and windbreak hedges are reported to have a neutral effect on groundnut yield at Bambey [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_10, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_14].

effect_mechanism: In high-income settings, agroforestry has been found both to raise and to lower output. Gains: in subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]; cited studies from Cañas, Costa Rica found milk production more than 15% higher for cows grazing silvopasture than in full sun and dry-season weight gains 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]; and a cited Costa Rican study found moderate shade gave coffee yields similar to, or 3% higher than, full sun [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4]. Losses: a cited Costa Rican experiment recorded a 30% coffee yield reduction in the shaded system against coffee monoculture [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. On Saskatchewan prairie fields lined with old field shelterbelts, cereal yields next to the belt were depressed out to about 10 m from the field edge in all 3 years, a competition effect; the sheltered zone beyond it gave above-average yields in 1989 and 1990, but in 1991, a season with well above average water availability, that beneficial zone was absent [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. conditionality: What separates the sides is the system and the competition for resources. The gains are livestock under tree cover and windbreak-sheltered vegetables in Ontario, where the plots were irrigated from ditches, whereas the losses are crops competing with trees: cereal next to Saskatchewan shelterbelts and established shade over coffee [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11]. Distance from the trees and the season separate them within the shelterbelt study: yields were depressed next to the belt every year, higher in the sheltered zone in 1989 and 1990, and showed no sheltered gain in the wet 1991 season [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. In Costa Rican coffee several units find no difference: a case study recorded no negative yield effect of shade, systems under 30 % shade cover did not differ in yield from full sun with management intensity driving yield instead, and young shaded coffee did not differ in fruiting nodes [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_2, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3, ev_crop_yield_villa20_2]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt units were measured in the field; their net loss uses the mid-field yield as the reference, a baseline the authors question [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. effect_mechanism: The units in this mixed-income cell measure different things and point different ways. A meta-analysis of shaded against conventional (unshaded) coffee and cocoa found productivity per hectare 26% lower in the shaded systems (p < 0.001) [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1]. A meta-analysis of plant hedgerows on sloping farmland found they significantly raised soil total nitrogen against farmland without hedgerows (standardized mean difference 1.33, 95% CI 0.98–1.68), soil nitrogen being read here as a component of the production gap [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1].
conditionality: The studies disagree, so the row states no direction. What separates them is both the practice and the outcome: the yield fall is the crop-specific cost of shade in perennial tree crops, measured as the crop harvest itself [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1], while the gain is a soil-fertility component under contour hedgerows, not a measured yield [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. The hedgerow pool mixes grass-only strips with woody hedgerows (vetiver and switchgrass alongside Leucaena, Gliricidia and Calliandra), so it is not woody-hedgerow-specific evidence [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. The shaded-crop unit is registered under a different source id but its file is the Jezeer et al. meta-analysis [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1]. For a project these readings are not interchangeable: higher soil nitrogen does not say that harvests rise, and lower shaded-crop yield per hectare does not count the other products of the shade trees.

effect_mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings, studies disagree on whether agroforestry narrows the production gap: livestock and sheltered-crop systems mostly gain, while crops intercropped with trees often lose output. Gains: wheat and barley intercropped 2.5 m from trees in Iran out-yielded monocultures by 35% and 39% [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2]; a meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland, alongside microclimatic improvements [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]; tree leaves added about 40 kg ha-1 of nitrogen in a Brazilian cactus pear and buffel grass system [ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]; and on the livestock side, Brazilian silvopasture gave higher daily bodyweight gain per animal, Colombian intensive silvopasture gave 32.1% more milk than the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, stocking reached 4.3 cows ha-1 while chemical fertiliser was eliminated, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Under drought, forage in a Colombian silvopastoral system stayed constant while grass monoculture biomass fell to 25%, deep-rooted trees give more stable dry-season forage, milk fell by 2.2% against 4.9% in conventional systems during El Niño events, and at El Hatico milk still rose 10% in 2009, the driest year in decades at 440 mm [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Losses: intercropped wheat in China and maize in Indonesia yielded significantly less than monocultures, and Brazilian soybean gave about 500 and 700 kg ha-1 against about 3000 and 2700 kg ha-1 in monoculture, attributed to lower radiation [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4, ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]; in a drip-irrigated trial in Xinjiang, China, soybean intercropped between juvenile plumcot rows yielded 46.03% less than sole-cropped soybean and intercropped alfalfa 51.83% less [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]; crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]; and dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. In perennial crops, shaded coffee in Paraná, Brazil yielded up to 101.99 kg/ha in its second year where the unshaded monoculture control yielded zero [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1], and a coconut review reports, second-hand, increased nut yields when pasture, black pepper and coffee were intercropped with coconut [ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1].
conditionality: Gains and losses both carry material weight, so no direction is stated; what separates them is visible in the evidence. Production system: the livestock and silvopasture units are almost all gains, while the losses are concentrated in crops intercropped with trees, where shading and competition reduce the crop [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3]; the Chinese plumcot losses were measured with the crop rows only about a metre from young trees [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1]. Distance and density: within one Chinese meta-analysis, yield rose across sheltered farmland but fell in the edge zone next to the trees, and the figures are not to be netted [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]; in Colombia, dense Acacia lowered milk per cow while sparser planting raised it [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. Management: the soybean loss is attributed to radiation, which the authors tie to pruning and management of the system [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]. For a Task Team Leader, the actionable distinctions are system type, tree spacing and density, and canopy management. On evidence quality, the plumcot intercrop is a direct randomised trial, while most other units on both sides are earlier results cited in Portuguese- or Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the shelterbelt meta-analysis is the main primary synthesis and supplies one figure on each side [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. The nitrogen unit is a soil-fertility component rather than a yield measure [ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7], and the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year, with the Colombian forage result likely describing the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Some silvopasture evidence also finds no difference: a systematic review of dairy silvopasture, mostly in Brazil, reports that the studies that evaluated milk production did not find a significant difference from treeless pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. Under shocks the perennial-crop evidence finds no shade effect either way: cocoa yield loss in the Bahian drought was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover, and Mexican coffee farms lost 18 to 40% of their harvest after a hurricane regardless of vegetation management [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The Paraná coffee result depends on tree species and development, and the coffee and coconut units are crop-specific [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1].

justification.mechanism: In upper-middle-income settings, studies disagree on whether agroforestry narrows the production gap: livestock and sheltered-crop systems mostly gain, while crops intercropped with trees often lose output. Gains: wheat and barley intercropped 2.5 m from trees in Iran out-yielded monocultures by 35% and 39% [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2]; a meta-analysis of Chinese farmland shelterbelts found crop yield 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland, alongside microclimatic improvements [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]; tree leaves added about 40 kg ha-1 of nitrogen in a Brazilian cactus pear and buffel grass system [ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]; and on the livestock side, Brazilian silvopasture gave higher daily bodyweight gain per animal, Colombian intensive silvopasture gave 32.1% more milk than the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, stocking reached 4.3 cows ha-1 while chemical fertiliser was eliminated, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Under drought, forage in a Colombian silvopastoral system stayed constant while grass monoculture biomass fell to 25%, deep-rooted trees give more stable dry-season forage, milk fell by 2.2% against 4.9% in conventional systems during El Niño events, and at El Hatico milk still rose 10% in 2009, the driest year in decades at 440 mm [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Losses: intercropped wheat in China and maize in Indonesia yielded significantly less than monocultures, and Brazilian soybean gave about 500 and 700 kg ha-1 against about 3000 and 2700 kg ha-1 in monoculture, attributed to lower radiation [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_4, ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]; in a drip-irrigated trial in Xinjiang, China, soybean intercropped between juvenile plumcot rows yielded 46.03% less than sole-cropped soybean and intercropped alfalfa 51.83% less [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]; crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]; and dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. In perennial crops, shaded coffee in Paraná, Brazil yielded up to 101.99 kg/ha in its second year where the unshaded monoculture control yielded zero [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1], and a coconut review reports, second-hand, increased nut yields when pasture, black pepper and coffee were intercropped with coconut [ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1].
justification.conditionality: Gains and losses both carry material weight, so no direction is stated; what separates them is visible in the evidence. Production system: the livestock and silvopasture units are almost all gains, while the losses are concentrated in crops intercropped with trees, where shading and competition reduce the crop [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_3]; the Chinese plumcot losses were measured with the crop rows only about a metre from young trees [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1]. Distance and density: within one Chinese meta-analysis, yield rose across sheltered farmland but fell in the edge zone next to the trees, and the figures are not to be netted [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2]; in Colombia, dense Acacia lowered milk per cow while sparser planting raised it [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. Management: the soybean loss is attributed to radiation, which the authors tie to pruning and management of the system [ev_crop_yield_santos25_5]. For a Task Team Leader, the actionable distinctions are system type, tree spacing and density, and canopy management. On evidence quality, the plumcot intercrop is a direct randomised trial, while most other units on both sides are earlier results cited in Portuguese- or Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the shelterbelt meta-analysis is the main primary synthesis and supplies one figure on each side [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_2, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1]. The nitrogen unit is a soil-fertility component rather than a yield measure [ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7], and the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year, with the Colombian forage result likely describing the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Some silvopasture evidence also finds no difference: a systematic review of dairy silvopasture, mostly in Brazil, reports that the studies that evaluated milk production did not find a significant difference from treeless pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. Under shocks the perennial-crop evidence finds no shade effect either way: cocoa yield loss in the Bahian drought was unrelated to shade-tree ground cover, and Mexican coffee farms lost 18 to 40% of their harvest after a hurricane regardless of vegetation management [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6]. The Paraná coffee result depends on tree species and development, and the coffee and coconut units are crop-specific [ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1].

effect_mechanism: Parkland trees make up a large share of high-quality livestock fodder, crucial in the dry season and during drought, and in Senegal access to cool zones under trees reduces livestock heat stress and so raises animal productivity [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22]. Under parkland trees, tuber yield is improved (+0.40 to +1.67 t ha-1) and legumes are less affected by tree cover [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1].
conditionality: Cereals lose out: grain yield ranged from a loss of 0.54 t ha-1 under Balanites aegyptiaca to a gain of 0.24 t ha-1 under F. albida, with reductions attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water, so the net effect depends on which crops dominate [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. All units are reviews citing earlier studies from the Sahel and Senegal, and the fodder and livestock gains are stated without a size [ev_forage_productivity_bayala14_1, ev_livestock_productivity_faosen24_22].

effect_mechanism: In irrigated cropping, trees compete with the crop for water, nutrients and light. Between rows of juvenile plumcot trees in drip-irrigated, semi-arid Xinjiang, China, intercropped soybean yielded 46.03% less and intercropped alfalfa 51.83% less than the same crops grown alone, over two years [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. In village irrigated perimeters of the Senegal River valley, hedges cut yields up to 10 metres from the hedge in the rainy season, while total yields across the protected plots rose 23 per cent in the off-season, as an FAO review reports from earlier work (Tamba; Samba et al.) [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13].
conditionality: The class rests on a single Chinese experiment with young trees, so confidence is low and the size may not hold as the trees mature or in other designs [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1]. Part of the Chinese loss reflects the smaller cropped area and the lower seeding rate and irrigation given to the intercropped soybean, and yields are per unit of total plot area, so the tree rows count against the crop [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_wang23_2]. The Senegal result runs the other way over the whole protected plot, which separates the two: hedges bordering a plot lose crop near the hedge but can raise the plot total, while trees planted through the plot at close spacing take crop area and water directly [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. The Senegal figure is a second-hand reading in grey literature with no comparator stated beyond the unprotected plots. China is upper-middle income, outside the LIC/LMIC target; Senegal is lower-middle income, within it [ev_crop_yield_wang23_1, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13].

effect_mechanism: In mixed crop–livestock systems, agroforestry's production gains come from several pathways. In Malawi, fertilizer-tree adopters had an average value of food crop production 35% higher than their counterfactual and maize productivity 32% higher [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1]. In Kenya's Lower Nyando, agroforestry-project farmers raised farm productivity by about 1,500 Ksh (US$19) a year more than a matched control group [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Across the Sahel (Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Senegal), moving from low-intensity to young-level farmer-managed natural regeneration significantly raised crop production and food consumption [ev_crop_yield_bina15_5]. In Brazilian silvopasture, cattle gained an average of 512 g of bodyweight per animal per day against 452 g/day in monoculture, a 60 g/day difference, and tree leaves added about 40 kg/ha of nitrogen in a cactus-pear/buffel-grass system, with potential to cut fertiliser cost [ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7].
conditionality: The class is capped at moderate rather than strong because only two of the seven units pointing this way state a size for the gain (the Malawi and Brazilian figures); the Kenyan, Sahelian and soil-nitrogen units describe direction without a comparable magnitude or, for Kenya, with standard errors the authors call large (P = 0.678) [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1, ev_crop_yield_bina15_5, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. Set against this, the same Malawi study finds non-adopters would be worse off if they adopted fertilizer trees — a decrease in productivity, significant for the value of food production though not for maize — which the engine counts as measured harm for some adopters [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_2]. A second Sahelian comparison, moving from low to continuous FMNR, found no significant difference, which the authors attribute to tree density and species quality rather than regeneration itself [ev_crop_yield_bina15_6]. The Malawi figures come from an ICRAF working paper evaluating an ICRAF-promoted technology, a conflict-of-interest the engine does not discount for the direction of this class but is noted here [ev_agricultural_production_value_coulibaly16_1, ev_crop_yield_coulibaly16_1].

effect_mechanism: In rangeland and pasture systems trees raise livestock output through forage, shade and higher stocking. In the Senegalese Ferlo, herbaceous biomass under Acacia tortilis and Balanites aegyptiaca canopies was 2 to 5 times that of treeless areas, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40 per cent of cattle and 80 per cent of small-ruminant diets late in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. In Latin American silvopasture, tree shade is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]; milk was 32.1% higher in intensive silvopasture than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Stocking rises up to four times above extensive grazing, reaching 4.3 cows ha-1 in a Colombian Leucaena system that eliminated chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1, ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Milk rose 29% on high tree-density pasture against low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture against full sun, with dry-season weight gains 2 to 5% higher [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Under drought, forage held constant in a Colombian silvopastoral system while grass-monoculture biomass fell to 25 %, deep-rooted trees give steadier dry-season forage, cattle are better fed in critical drought periods, milk fell by 2.2% against 4.9% in conventional systems during El Niño events, and at El Hatico milk still rose 10% in 2009, the driest year in decades (440 mm) [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2, ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4].
conditionality: The row carries a harm signal tied to tree density: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture (1110 trees/ha) gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field, while the low-density stand (407 trees/ha) gave 16.6 L [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. Not every comparison finds a milk gain: a systematic review of mostly Brazilian dairy silvopasture found that the studies which measured milk production did not find a significant difference from treeless pasture, even where trees altered the thermal environment [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. What separates that null from the gains, as far as the evidence says, is the system: the gains come mostly from intensive silvopasture with fodder shrubs such as Leucaena and Tithonia, where the trees add feed as well as shade, while the Brazilian studies compare shade from exotic trees against treeless pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. Apart from that review, every unit is an earlier study read second-hand through a FAO country assessment, Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume, and none is a pastoral-system experiment run by the citing authors [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3]. The Senegalese diet shares describe how much of the ration comes from trees, not a measured production change [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. Most of the Latin American evidence is intensive silvopasture with Leucaena shrubs in upper-middle-income Colombia, the Brazilian review is upper-middle income, and the Costa Rican units are high-income; milk gains attributed to heat relief also reflect extra foliage and fruit [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1]. The El Hatico result is a single farm compared year on year, and the Colombian drought-forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1].
