justification.mechanism: In rangeland and pasture systems trees raise livestock output through forage, shade and higher stocking. In the Senegalese Ferlo, herbaceous biomass under Acacia tortilis and Balanites aegyptiaca canopies was 2 to 5 times that of treeless areas, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40 per cent of cattle and 80 per cent of small-ruminant diets late in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. In Latin American silvopasture, tree shade is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4]; milk was 32.1% higher in intensive silvopasture than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Stocking rises up to four times above extensive grazing, reaching 4.3 cows ha-1 in a Colombian Leucaena system that eliminated chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1, ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. Milk rose 29% on high tree-density pasture against low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture against full sun, with dry-season weight gains 2 to 5% higher [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Under drought, forage held constant in a Colombian silvopastoral system while grass-monoculture biomass fell to 25 %, deep-rooted trees give steadier dry-season forage, cattle are better fed in critical drought periods, milk fell by 2.2% against 4.9% in conventional systems during El Niño events, and at El Hatico milk still rose 10% in 2009, the driest year in decades (440 mm) [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2, ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4].
justification.conditionality: The row carries a harm signal tied to tree density: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture (1110 trees/ha) gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field, while the low-density stand (407 trees/ha) gave 16.6 L [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. Not every comparison finds a milk gain: a systematic review of mostly Brazilian dairy silvopasture found that the studies which measured milk production did not find a significant difference from treeless pasture, even where trees altered the thermal environment [ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. What separates that null from the gains, as far as the evidence says, is the system: the gains come mostly from intensive silvopasture with fodder shrubs such as Leucaena and Tithonia, where the trees add feed as well as shade, while the Brazilian studies compare shade from exotic trees against treeless pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_deniz23_1]. Apart from that review, every unit is an earlier study read second-hand through a FAO country assessment, Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume, and none is a pastoral-system experiment run by the citing authors [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3]. The Senegalese diet shares describe how much of the ration comes from trees, not a measured production change [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21]. Most of the Latin American evidence is intensive silvopasture with Leucaena shrubs in upper-middle-income Colombia, the Brazilian review is upper-middle income, and the Costa Rican units are high-income; milk gains attributed to heat relief also reflect extra foliage and fruit [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1]. The El Hatico result is a single farm compared year on year, and the Colombian drought-forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1].

effect_mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis reports crop yield under agroforestry about twice that of non-agroforestry controls in the humid zone, and a pantropical meta-analysis finds higher soil nitrogen stocks than in crop monocultures, used here as a component [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. A meta-analysis cited in Arslan et al. (Branca et al.) associates agroforestry techniques with a 69% increase in cereal yields across the studies it consulted [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. IPCC assessments attribute higher land-equivalent ratios and large food-production benefits to well-planned agroforestry, and a cited review reports agroforestry systems 36-100% more productive than monoculture [ev_crop_yield_ipccar6ch5_8, ev_crop_yield_ipccsrccl6_3, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_12]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers in an agroforestry project improved farm productivity on average against a control group [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of agroforestry adoption by smallholders in sub-Saharan Africa found a significant yield gain for maize in the high-quality studies (Cohen's d = 0.27, 95% CI: 0.12 to 0.42), and a pan-tropical meta-analysis of pest control reports that the only studies testing whether agroforestry pest control translated into crop yield both found a gain [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2, ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1].
conditionality: A systematic review's pooled crop-yield effect has a confidence interval spanning zero, the sub-Saharan adoption meta-analysis found that agroforestry overall is not associated with a statistically significant effect on yield (Cohen's d = 0.35, 95% CI: −0.07 to 0.78) [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1], an integrative review counts 15 of 21 studies favouring agroforestry and 5 favouring monoculture, and another review notes trade-offs between crop intensification and ecosystem services in most agroforestry [ev_crop_yield_castle21s_1, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_1, ev_crop_yield_vannoordwijk21_7]. The strong class therefore holds for well-designed tree–crop systems and for the better-quality studies; pooled adoption effects across all study types are smaller and less certain [ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_1, ev_crop_yield_jemaneh26_2]. The pest-control yield link rests on very few studies cited in the meta-analysis (Ogol, Spence and Keddie 1999; Sileshi et al. 2005) [ev_crop_yield_pumarino15_1]. The cited 69% cereal-yield figure reaches this row second-hand through Arslan et al.: the citing text does not describe the agroforestry techniques further and reports no significance [ev_crop_yield_arsl15_14]. The pooled magnitude combines a crop-yield and a soil-nitrogen response ratio [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_muchane20_1]. The Lower Nyando productivity gain had large standard errors and was not significant [ev_agricultural_production_value_thorlak12_1]. Livestock yield under linear agroforestry (alleys and windbreaks pooled) in a global review did not differ from the control: a 0.3% reduction with an even split of gains and losses over 36 paddock years [ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_13].

effect_mechanism: Linear tree plantings have been found both to raise and to lower yields. Gains come from shelter: windbreaks are reported to raise wheat yields by 15 to 20% by protecting plants from winter desiccation, protected plots in the Senegal River valley showed a 23 per cent total yield increase in the off-season, crop yield was 16.57% higher within sheltered farmland in a Chinese shelterbelt meta-analysis, and live fences can improve soil fertility and crop yields provided tree roots are deeper than crop roots [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_7, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13, ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_moran18_11]. In subarctic Ontario, a site lined by willow windbreaks produced about 300 g/m2 of bean pods against about 60 g/m2 at an open site, and potato tuber yield was 33% greater (3200 versus 2400 g/m2) [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. A meta-analysis of plant hedgerows found they raised soil total N (SMD = 1.33; 95% CI 0.98–1.68), counted here as a component of the production gap; hedgerow litter and the capture of nutrient-laden sediment from runoff supply it [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1]. Losses come from competition and shade: crop yield in shelterbelt edge zones fell by an average of 20.47% [ev_crop_yield_hao26_2], cereal yields next to Saskatchewan shelterbelts were depressed out to about 10 m from the field edge in all 3 years of a field study [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1], excess shade can reduce pasture productivity [ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14], and in the West African Sahel live fences and fodder banks reduced yields in the first year [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Hedgerow intercropping in a sub-Saharan meta-analysis gave a response ratio of 0.9, an interval touching no effect [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]. A global quantitative review of paddocks with windbreaks found yield reduced by 8.3% on average against paddocks with no windbreaks, excluding the land occupied by the trees, with more decreases (n = 171) than increases (n = 83): crop yield −9.2% and crop biomass −9.3%, while pasture showed a small average increase of +3.1% [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_2, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_3, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_4]. In the same Saskatchewan study the sheltered zone beyond the competition strip gave above-average yields in 1989 and 1990, but against the mid-field yield the authors estimate a net field yield loss equal to the width of the shelterbelt, while doubting that baseline [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_4]. The global review's distance-response curves nonetheless predict a total yield change of +8.04% across a paddock 20 tree heights wide [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5].
conditionality: The evidence itself names most of what separates gains from losses. Distance from the trees: the same Chinese meta-analysis reports the field-scale gain and the edge-zone loss, which are not to be netted [ev_crop_yield_hao26_1, ev_crop_yield_hao26_2], and in Senegal yields fell within 10 metres of the hedges in the rainy season while the protected plots as a whole gained [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_13]. Root depth: the live-fence benefit is conditional on tree roots lying deeper than crop roots [ev_crop_yield_moran18_11]. Season: in the Saskatchewan study the sheltered-zone gain appeared in 1989 and 1990 but was absent in 1991, a season with well above average water availability, which the authors attribute to high actual evapotranspiration by the crops [ev_crop_yield_kowa95_2, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_3]. Time: the Sahel live-fence penalty was in the first year and yields recovered in the second [ev_crop_yield_lasco14_2]. Shade level: the pasture loss is from excess shade [ev_livestock_productivity_moran18_14]. These point to actionable design choices: species with deep roots, spacing and shade control, and accepting a first-year dip. At Bambey windbreak hedges had a neutral effect on groundnut [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_14]. On evidence quality, the hedgerow estimate is close to no effect rather than a clear loss [ev_crop_yield_kuyah19_5]; most other units are cited secondary results, the wheat figure has no stated location, and the Saskatchewan shelterbelt units are measured but high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_dobhal24_7, ev_crop_yield_moran18_11, ev_crop_yield_kowa95_1]. Paddock geometry: the same review gives a pooled paddock loss and a predicted gain across a paddock 20 tree heights wide, so the width of the sheltered paddock relative to tree height separates loss from gain in its own data, consistent with the distance effect above [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1, ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_5]. Crop type: in that review crop yield and biomass fell while pasture rose slightly, although the difference between yield types was not significant [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_2, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_4]. The global review's main text gives no country or income-group breakdown, so its losses cannot be placed against the LIC/LMIC target, and its windbreak group also takes in hedgerows and native forest blocks [ev_crop_yield_baker25h2_1]. The Ontario windbreak gain is high-income boreal evidence from a single windbreak-lined site against a single open site, with plots irrigated from ditches, so it does not test competition next to the trees [ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_1, ev_crop_yield_barbeau18_2]. The hedgerow soil-nitrogen pool mixes grass-only strips with woody hedgerows and measures soil concentration, not yield, so it shows a pathway to higher output rather than the output itself [ev_soil_nitrogen_zheng20_1].

justification.statement: agroforestry production_gap: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. effect_mechanism: Regeneration-based farmland (FMNR and parkland systems) raises crop production mainly through nutrient addition under tree canopies and direct yield gains at the plot level. In Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded 23-26% more grain than open-field wheat in normal seasons (2013-2014), and up to 85% more in El Niño 2015, a dry year when both yields were low; available mineral nitrogen close to the crowns was 35-55% larger than under sole wheat [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_1]. In Senegal, millet yields are reported to double or even triple under F. albida canopy, and a meta-analysis reports mean yield increases of 150% for maize and 73% for sorghum under its canopy, alongside a significant 50% rise in total soil nitrogen, 21% in phosphorus and 32% in potassium [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9, ev_soil_nitrogen_faosen24_2]. At Nioro-du-Rip, Senegal, millet grain yield with Piliostigma reticulatum was 886 kg/ha against 499 kg/ha without, at zero NPK [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_15], and yields (millet and groundnut, plus fruit and wood) are higher on plots where intensive FMNR is practised [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_14]. In Niger, soil nitrogen concentration was 38% higher under scattered shrubs than in open fields [ev_soil_nitrogen_felix18_1], and a pan-Sahelian review of 26 parkland references found millet and sorghum yields often higher in the presence of shrubs, ranging -25 to +120% [ev_crop_yield_felix18_1]; in Maradi, Niger, millet yields rose 120 to 209 kg/ha where FMNR was older than six years, and FMNR is estimated to have raised yields by an average of 100 kg/ha across 5 million hectares [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3]. In Honduras, the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system raised maize yields from 1.9 to 3.2 t/ha and bean yields from 0.8 to 2.0 t/ha against the prior slash-and-burn system [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_2], and farmers report maize yield increases of a minimum of 60%, with the longest-running Quesungual fields averaging 2.9 t/ha against a best previous yield of 1.6 t/ha on the same steep, poor-soil fields [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6]. In Ghana, 60% of FMNR-practising households reported increased farm yield from the same plot of land [ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1]. In the Sahel, moving from low to young-level FMNR significantly raised crop production [ev_crop_yield_bina15_5]. For livestock, herbaceous biomass under tree canopy in Senegal's Ferlo was 2 to 5 times that in treeless areas, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40% of cattle diet and 80% of small-ruminant diet in the dry-to-wet-season transition [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21].
conditionality: Against this, the same Senegalese source reports measured harm: groundnut and millet yields fell under Cordyla pinnata canopy compared with outside the cover [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11], and under parkland trees generally, cereal grain yield ranged from a loss under Balanites aegyptiaca to only a small gain under Faidherbia albida, attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water, while legumes were less affected and tubers improved [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. Groundnut under F. albida itself behaves inconsistently across studies — one found a significant pod-yield rise, another variable yields, a third yield decreases [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_10]. In Niger, FMNR did not significantly raise cereal grain yields, with the authors attributing any income gain instead to crop diversification into higher-value crops [ev_crop_yield_haglund11_1], and moving from low to continuous FMNR gave no significant production gain in the Sahel, which the authors attribute to tree density and species quality [ev_crop_yield_bina15_6]. The pan-Sahelian parkland review that found yield gains under shrubs also found more variability under trees specifically, ranging from complete crop failure (-100%) to a tripling (+200%) [ev_crop_yield_felix18_2]. The Ethiopian temperature-cooling pathway only translated to a yield response once nitrogen was applied; without it, simulated wheat yield did not respond to the cooling at all, and total soil nitrogen itself showed no significant difference under versus outside the canopy at the end of one season despite the larger available nitrogen measured close to the crowns [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_2]. The Honduran and Ghanaian figures are farmer reports or project self-evaluations relayed by project-promoter staff or grey literature, not independently verified, and the Honduran comparator is the single best prior yield on the same fields, not an average [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6, ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1]. All units sit in low and lower-middle-income West African and Central American drylands, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_felix18_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1].

justification.mechanism: Regeneration-based farmland (FMNR and parkland systems) raises crop production mainly through nutrient addition under tree canopies and direct yield gains at the plot level. In Ethiopia, wheat under Faidherbia albida crowns yielded 23-26% more grain than open-field wheat in normal seasons (2013-2014), and up to 85% more in El Niño 2015, a dry year when both yields were low; available mineral nitrogen close to the crowns was 35-55% larger than under sole wheat [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_sida18_2, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_1]. In Senegal, millet yields are reported to double or even triple under F. albida canopy, and a meta-analysis reports mean yield increases of 150% for maize and 73% for sorghum under its canopy, alongside a significant 50% rise in total soil nitrogen, 21% in phosphorus and 32% in potassium [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_8, ev_crop_yield_faosen24_9, ev_soil_nitrogen_faosen24_2]. At Nioro-du-Rip, Senegal, millet grain yield with Piliostigma reticulatum was 886 kg/ha against 499 kg/ha without, at zero NPK [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_15], and yields (millet and groundnut, plus fruit and wood) are higher on plots where intensive FMNR is practised [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_14]. In Niger, soil nitrogen concentration was 38% higher under scattered shrubs than in open fields [ev_soil_nitrogen_felix18_1], and a pan-Sahelian review of 26 parkland references found millet and sorghum yields often higher in the presence of shrubs, ranging -25 to +120% [ev_crop_yield_felix18_1]; in Maradi, Niger, millet yields rose 120 to 209 kg/ha where FMNR was older than six years, and FMNR is estimated to have raised yields by an average of 100 kg/ha across 5 million hectares [ev_crop_yield_abasse23_1, ev_crop_yield_abasse23_3]. In Honduras, the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system raised maize yields from 1.9 to 3.2 t/ha and bean yields from 0.8 to 2.0 t/ha against the prior slash-and-burn system [ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_2], and farmers report maize yield increases of a minimum of 60%, with the longest-running Quesungual fields averaging 2.9 t/ha against a best previous yield of 1.6 t/ha on the same steep, poor-soil fields [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6]. In Ghana, 60% of FMNR-practising households reported increased farm yield from the same plot of land [ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1]. In the Sahel, moving from low to young-level FMNR significantly raised crop production [ev_crop_yield_bina15_5]. For livestock, herbaceous biomass under tree canopy in Senegal's Ferlo was 2 to 5 times that in treeless areas, and tree leaves, fruit and pods make up about 40% of cattle diet and 80% of small-ruminant diet in the dry-to-wet-season transition [ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_20, ev_forage_productivity_faosen24_21].
justification.conditionality: Against this, the same Senegalese source reports measured harm: groundnut and millet yields fell under Cordyla pinnata canopy compared with outside the cover [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_11], and under parkland trees generally, cereal grain yield ranged from a loss under Balanites aegyptiaca to only a small gain under Faidherbia albida, attributed to competition for light, nutrients and water, while legumes were less affected and tubers improved [ev_crop_yield_bayala14_1]. Groundnut under F. albida itself behaves inconsistently across studies — one found a significant pod-yield rise, another variable yields, a third yield decreases [ev_crop_yield_faosen24_10]. In Niger, FMNR did not significantly raise cereal grain yields, with the authors attributing any income gain instead to crop diversification into higher-value crops [ev_crop_yield_haglund11_1], and moving from low to continuous FMNR gave no significant production gain in the Sahel, which the authors attribute to tree density and species quality [ev_crop_yield_bina15_6]. The pan-Sahelian parkland review that found yield gains under shrubs also found more variability under trees specifically, ranging from complete crop failure (-100%) to a tripling (+200%) [ev_crop_yield_felix18_2]. The Ethiopian temperature-cooling pathway only translated to a yield response once nitrogen was applied; without it, simulated wheat yield did not respond to the cooling at all, and total soil nitrogen itself showed no significant difference under versus outside the canopy at the end of one season despite the larger available nitrogen measured close to the crowns [ev_crop_yield_sida18_3, ev_crop_yield_sida18_4, ev_soil_nitrogen_sida18_2]. The Honduran and Ghanaian figures are farmer reports or project self-evaluations relayed by project-promoter staff or grey literature, not independently verified, and the Honduran comparator is the single best prior yield on the same fields, not an average [ev_crop_yield_welc02_5, ev_crop_yield_welc02_6, ev_crop_yield_talensi21_1]. All units sit in low and lower-middle-income West African and Central American drylands, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_crop_yield_sida18_1, ev_crop_yield_felix18_1, ev_crop_yield_chaudhury11_1].

effect_mechanism: Shade trees over coffee and cocoa have been found both to raise and to lower production. Gains: a coffee meta-analysis found agroforestry reduced the odds of climate-related yield loss (OR = 0.69) and improved continuous outcomes such as yield and bean quality (SMD = +0.42) against conventional systems [ev_crop_yield_patil25_1, ev_crop_yield_patil25_2]; a cocoa meta-analysis found total system yields about ten times higher than in monocultures, and a Bolivian cocoa study cited second-hand found total production three times higher [ev_crop_yield_niether20_2, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_9]; in Ethiopian smallholder coffee, leguminous shade and canopy openness benefited yields, including in the El Niño shock years [ev_crop_yield_morel24_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_3]; and second-hand reports cite moderate shade yielding up to 3% more than full-sun coffee, reduced biennial yield oscillation, lower yield variability under diverse shade, intercropped coconut yielding more nuts, nitrogen fixation around 100 kg ha-1 by Erythrina or Inga shade, and in Paraná shaded coffee yielding up to 101.99 kg/ha where the unshaded control yielded zero [ev_crop_yield_villa20_4, ev_yield_stability_montagnini15_1, ev_crop_yield_morel24_4, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_1, ev_soil_nitrogen_villa20_12, ev_crop_yield_robusti17_1]. In southern Rwanda, sowing the legume shrub Tephrosia vogelii in the alleys of smallholder coffee and applying it as mulch raised coffee yield by 23–36% over the trial, a further 25–42% when NPK fertilizer was added, though the gain was statistically significant only in the first season [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1, ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_2]. Losses: main-crop yield per hectare was 26% lower in shaded coffee and cocoa than conventional systems and cocoa yields 25% lower than in monocultures [ev_crop_yield_jezeer17_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_1]; second-hand reports cite cocoa productivity 41% higher in monocultures, a 30% coffee yield reduction once shade was established, 41% fewer coffee fruits under 40 to 60% Erythrina shade, significant productivity reductions under Organic-certified shade coffee, and a cocoa yield ceiling at high carbon storage [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6, ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_11, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_4, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6].
conditionality: What separates the sides, in the sources' own terms, is first what is counted and second how much shade. The gains in total system output count the by-crops and timber, while the losses are in the main crop alone: the same cocoa meta-analysis reports cocoa yields 25% lower but total system yields about ten times higher [ev_crop_yield_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_niether20_2]. Shade density: coffee yields declined under >60% shade with 30 to 60% shade most favourable, fruit set fell under 40 to 60% Erythrina cover, and shaded systems under 30 % cover did not differ from full sun, management intensity driving yield instead [ev_crop_yield_patil25_3, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1, ev_crop_yield_villa20_3]. Drought does not reliably favour shade: in the Ghanaian experiment shade did not prevent the drought-induced cocoa yield decline [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2], cited work reports tree–cacao water competition pushing yields below open-sun levels [ev_crop_yield_watts22_8], Bahian cocoa drought losses were unrelated to shade-tree cover and Mexican hurricane harvest losses unrelated to shade management [ev_crop_yield_gateau18_2, ev_crop_yield_philpott08_6], and diverse shade showed no direct benefit in the El Niño shock [ev_crop_yield_morel24_2]. Several units find no difference: in a Costa Rican case study no yield loss from shade was recorded, coconut yields are not strongly affected by interspace trees except where they block light, galangal yield was unaffected by over-canopy, soil nitrogen did not differ in cocoa systems, and young shaded coffee did not differ in fruiting nodes [ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_2, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_2, ev_crop_yield_kumar22_3, ev_soil_nitrogen_niether20_1, ev_crop_yield_villa20_2]; the coffee meta-regression found no moderator, shade density included, that significantly explained the variance [ev_crop_yield_patil25_9]. The evidence is crop-specific to coffee, cocoa and coconut; the Rwandan Tephrosia gain comes from a mulch-producing legume intercrop rather than from shade trees [ev_crop_yield_bucagu13_1]; the Ghanaian shade came from nets rather than trees, and the certification loss bundles shade with Organic certification rather than isolating it [ev_crop_yield_mensah23_2, ev_crop_yield_castle21s_4]. Many units are earlier studies read second-hand through Portuguese-, Spanish- or French-language reviews [ev_crop_yield_dsantos23_6, ev_crop_yield_villa20_1, ev_crop_yield_seghieri19_6].

justification.statement: agroforestry production_gap: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: adjacent).

effect_mechanism: Trees in pasture have been found both to raise and to lower production. Gains, mostly from Latin American intensive silvopasture and shaded pastures: Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain, Brazilian silvopasture gave a higher mean bodyweight gain per animal (512 g day-1) than monoculture (452 g day-1), and tree leaves added about 40 kg ha-1 of nitrogen in a Brazilian semi-arid system [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. In Colombian intensive silvopasture, milk production was 32.1% higher than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture raises stocking rates up to four times above extensive grazing and with them meat and milk output per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1]. In Colombia, a Leucaena-based silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows ha-1 while eliminating chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During El Niño events, milk production fell by 2.2% in silvopastoral systems against 4.9% in conventional systems [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture compared with full sun, and dry-season weight gains were 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Losses come from a global quantitative review of dispersed trees in pasture: pasture yield fell by 20.8% on average against control plots, by a predicted 30% where tree density exceeded 800 trees per hectare, and to below 50% of the control under the oldest trees, while livestock yield fell by 18.6% on average, declining with more trees up to ~300 trees per hectare and with increasing tree age [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_16].
conditionality: The Brazilian and humid-tropic units are cited secondary results, adjacent to the LIC/LMIC target; the nitrogen unit is a component rather than a productivity measure [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. Tree density matters: dense Acacia decurrens silvopasture gave 14.3 L of milk per cow per day against 15 L in the open field [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_2]. The Latin American livestock units are earlier studies cited in Spanish-language reviews or a CATIE edited volume; the El Hatico milk result is a single farm compared year on year and the Colombian forage result likely describes the same farm [ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4, ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1]. justification.mechanism: Trees in pasture have been found both to raise and to lower production. Gains, mostly from Latin American intensive silvopasture and shaded pastures: Tree shade in pastures is associated with 13 to 28% increases in milk production and weight gain, Brazilian silvopasture gave a higher mean bodyweight gain per animal (512 g day-1) than monoculture (452 g day-1), and tree leaves added about 40 kg ha-1 of nitrogen in a Brazilian semi-arid system [ev_livestock_productivity_murg13_4, ev_livestock_productivity_santos25_12, ev_soil_nitrogen_santos25_7]. In Colombian intensive silvopasture, milk production was 32.1% higher than with the same grasses without shrubs or trees, milk per hectare rose from 2 540 to 4 528 L a year with Leucaena, and silvopasture is cited as producing 12 times more beef than traditional grazing [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_3, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_1, ev_livestock_productivity_saucedo23_3]. Intensive silvopasture raises stocking rates up to four times above extensive grazing and with them meat and milk output per hectare [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_1]. In Colombia, a Leucaena-based silvopastoral system raised stocking to 4.3 cows ha-1 while eliminating chemical fertiliser [ev_livestock_productivity_cisneros24_1]. In Colombia, forage production in a silvopastoral system of pastures, trees and Leucaena shrubs stayed constant in periods of intense drought while biomass in grass monoculture fell to 25%, and deep-rooted silvopasture trees are more drought-tolerant and give more stable forage volumes in the dry season [ev_forage_productivity_cisneros24_1, ev_forage_productivity_saucedo23_1]. Cattle in intensive silvopasture are better fed in critical drought periods, which reduces seasonal reproduction crises [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_2]. During El Niño events, milk production fell by 2.2% in silvopastoral systems against 4.9% in conventional systems [ev_livestock_productivity_guaqueta25_1]. At El Hatico, Colombia, the switch to intensive silvopasture allowed pasture irrigation to be dropped, and in 2009, the year with the lowest rainfall in several decades (440 mm), milk production still rose 10% on the previous year [ev_livestock_productivity_montagnini15_4]. Milk production rose 29% for cows on pasture with high tree density compared with low tree cover and above 15% in silvopasture compared with full sun, and dry-season weight gains were 2 to 5% higher on high tree-density pasture [ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_1, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_2, ev_livestock_productivity_navas10_3]. Losses come from a global quantitative review of dispersed trees in pasture: pasture yield fell by 20.8% on average against control plots, by a predicted 30% where tree density exceeded 800 trees per hectare, and to below 50% of the control under the oldest trees, while livestock yield fell by 18.6% on average, declining with more trees up to ~300 trees per hectare and with increasing tree age [ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_9, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_10, ev_forage_productivity_baker25h2_12, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_14, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_15, ev_livestock_productivity_baker25h2_16].

effect_mechanism: Across sub-practices, agroforestry mostly raises household income and economic returns, with silvopastoral systems showing the strongest and most consistent gains. In Colombia, production costs were US$127/ha lower on average under intensive silvopastoral systems than traditional ranching, and the switch raised farmers' annual income by as much as US$523/ha [ev_household_income_cmscr20_6]; milk-sales income rose 42.12% under silvopasture, driven by higher stocking capacity (2.71 vs 1.84 animal units) [ev_household_income_montagnini15_1], and a benefit-cost ratio of 2.8 was found for an intensive silvopastoral system against 1.34 for a traditional system [ev_economic_return_saucedo23_1]. In shaded coffee and cocoa, a meta-analysis found net returns 23% higher on average in shaded systems, and a trend toward a higher benefit-cost ratio (1.66 against 1.44 for conventional systems) [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_1, ev_economic_return_jezeer17_2]. In India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea agroforestry system gave net returns 1.67 to 2.72 times higher than the same species grown alone, with a benefit-cost ratio up to 2.33, and eucalyptus coppice agroforestry gave a benefit-cost ratio of 3.5:1 for the first rotation, rising in subsequent rotations as coppicing costs fall [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1, ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3]. In Sudan, Acacia senegal intercropped with sorghum, sesame and roselle gave higher net revenue than any sole crop in a partial-budget analysis [ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_fadl13_5, ev_economic_return_fadl13_6]. In Kenya, improved-fallow agroforestry raised returns to labour to about US$2.17 a day, 33% higher than continuous maize with no inputs [ev_economic_return_place05_3]. In Nigeria, intercropping sweet orange with chilli pepper and amaranthus, or cassava and maize, gave a positive net present value against a negative NPV for monocropped orange [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1]. Overall meta-analytic reviews find a positive but often small average effect: one puts the effect of agroforestry adoption on income at Cohen's d = 0.28 [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1], and another at a standardised mean difference of 0.12, ranging up to 0.52 for a Kenyan climate-vulnerability-reduction programme [ev_household_income_castle21s_1, ev_household_income_castle21s_2]. In Nepal, the share of households below the poverty line fell from 48% in 2013 to 34% in 2016 after a market-oriented agroforestry intervention, with the steepest drop (62% to 28%) in one community [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1].
conditionality: Against this, several units find losses or no effect. In Brazil, an agroforestry system's rice component showed negative economic performance needing adjustment, black pepper also turned unprofitable in low-price cycles, and a vegetable-heavy system collapsed from its seventh year through poor long-term management [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_5]. The same standardised-mean-difference review that found a 0.52 gain in Kenya found a −0.29 effect for crop-fruit tree intercropping in China [ev_household_income_castle21s_2], and in Nigeria, cut-and-carry mulching from multipurpose trees is profitable only where land and labour are abundant, turning unprofitable with negative returns where land is scarce [ev_economic_return_korm99_6]. In cocoa agroforestry across ten countries, total system production was higher than in monoculture but this was not reflected in higher revenues, net present values or lower costs [ev_economic_return_niether20_1]. In Ecuador, technified (less-shaded, more input-intensive) coffee management achieved the highest net margin per hectare against traditional, semi-intensive and organic (more-shaded) management — a signal that intensifying away from shade can out-earn the more agroforestry-like systems [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1]. The Regreening Africa endline found more households selling tree products (rising from 8% to 20% overall, and sharply in Ghana and Mali), but average household income from tree products did not change overall, remaining at USD 82 (PPP) with wide variation by country [ev_household_income_rgaf23_6]. The World Bank's Colombian project found 47.2% of beneficiaries below the poverty line at baseline and could not yet attribute a clear poverty reduction, since many silvopastoral systems were still in their establishment phase and project effects were hard to separate from drought and other factors [ev_rural_poverty_cmscr20_9]. Most of the clearest gains (Colombia, Costa Rica, Sahel, Central America) sit inside the LIC/LMIC target, while the Ecuadorian, Chinese and Indonesian counter-signals sit in varied income contexts, so the row's strength is read from this balance rather than any single study [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1, ev_household_income_castle21s_2, ev_economic_return_castle21s_4].

In shaded coffee and cocoa, a meta-analysis found net returns 23% higher on average in shaded systems, and a trend toward a higher benefit-cost ratio (1.66 against 1.44 for conventional systems) [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_1, ev_economic_return_jezeer17_2]. In India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea agroforestry system gave net returns 1.67 to 2.72 times higher than the same species grown alone, with a benefit-cost ratio up to 2.33, and eucalyptus coppice agroforestry gave a benefit-cost ratio of 3.5:1 for the first rotation, rising in subsequent rotations as coppicing costs fall [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1, ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3]. In Sudan, Acacia senegal intercropped with sorghum, sesame and roselle gave higher net revenue than any sole crop in a partial-budget analysis [ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_fadl13_5, ev_economic_return_fadl13_6]. In Kenya, improved-fallow agroforestry raised returns to labour to about US$2.17 a day, 33% higher than continuous maize with no inputs [ev_economic_return_place05_3]. In Nigeria, intercropping sweet orange with chilli pepper and amaranthus, or cassava and maize, gave a positive net present value against a negative NPV for monocropped orange [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1]. Overall meta-analytic reviews find a positive but often small average effect: one puts the effect of agroforestry adoption on income at Cohen's d = 0.28 [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1], and another at a standardised mean difference of 0.12, ranging up to 0.52 for a Kenyan climate-vulnerability-reduction programme [ev_household_income_castle21s_1, ev_household_income_castle21s_2]. In Nepal, the share of households below the poverty line fell from 48% in 2013 to 34% in 2016 after a market-oriented agroforestry intervention, with the steepest drop (62% to 28%) in one community [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1].
justification.conditionality: Against this, several units find losses or no effect. In Brazil, an agroforestry system's rice component showed negative economic performance needing adjustment, black pepper also turned unprofitable in low-price cycles, and a vegetable-heavy system collapsed from its seventh year through poor long-term management [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_5]. The same standardised-mean-difference review that found a 0.52 gain in Kenya found a −0.29 effect for crop-fruit tree intercropping in China [ev_household_income_castle21s_2], and in Nigeria, cut-and-carry mulching from multipurpose trees is profitable only where land and labour are abundant, turning unprofitable with negative returns where land is scarce [ev_economic_return_korm99_6]. In cocoa agroforestry across ten countries, total system production was higher than in monoculture but this was not reflected in higher revenues, net present values or lower costs [ev_economic_return_niether20_1]. In Ecuador, technified (less-shaded, more input-intensive) coffee management achieved the highest net margin per hectare against traditional, semi-intensive and organic (more-shaded) management — a signal that intensifying away from shade can out-earn the more agroforestry-like systems [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1]. The Regreening Africa endline found more households selling tree products (rising from 8% to 20% overall, and sharply in Ghana and Mali), but average household income from tree products did not change overall, remaining at USD 82 (PPP) with wide variation by country [ev_household_income_rgaf23_6]. The World Bank's Colombian project found 47.2% of beneficiaries below the poverty line at baseline and could not yet attribute a clear poverty reduction, since many silvopastoral systems were still in their establishment phase and project effects were hard to separate from drought and other factors [ev_rural_poverty_cmscr20_9]. Most of the clearest gains (Colombia, Costa Rica, Sahel, Central America) sit inside the LIC/LMIC target, while the Ecuadorian, Chinese and Indonesian counter-signals sit in varied income contexts, so the row's strength is read from this balance rather than any single study [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1, ev_household_income_castle21s_2, ev_economic_return_castle21s_4].

effect_mechanism: In irrigated cropland, trees bring returns from wood, fodder or fruit on top of the crop. A Senegalese review cites Fall et al. (2002) estimating that in the Senegal River valley a windbreak hedge in irrigated rice had an internal rate of return of 36 per cent, or 58 per cent when the woody products of the hedge were counted (Satin, 1998) [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15]. In canal-irrigated waterlogged fields at Hisar, India, a biodrainage review cites a study by Ram et al. finding a benefit–cost ratio of 3.5: 1 for the first rotation of Eucalyptus boundary strips, with returns from fodder, wood or fibre after only an initial investment [ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3]. In a drip-irrigated trial in Xinjiang, China, juvenile plumcot trees intercropped with alfalfa or soybean gave a higher average cash flow than the corresponding sole crops [ev_economic_return_wang23_1].
conditionality: How big the poverty effect is cannot be stated: the units report returns on investment or cash flow, components of household income rather than measured poverty change. The Senegalese and Indian figures are earlier studies read second-hand in reviews, and the Indian ratio is expected to rise in later rotations because coppiced Eucalyptus costs little to regrow [ev_economic_return_faosen24_15, ev_economic_return_singhlal18_3]. The Chinese trial covers only the establishment years, and in the same trial the intercropped soybean and alfalfa yielded much less than sole crops, so the cash-flow gain comes from the fruit trees rather than from the crop [ev_economic_return_wang23_1]. The evidence comes from lower-middle-income Senegal and India and upper-middle-income China.

effect_mechanism: An East African systematic review counts income among the main livelihood benefits of agroforestry, diversifying rural livelihoods and acting as a safety net in climate shocks, and calliandra fodder raised dairy farmers' net income in Kenya and Uganda [ev_household_income_muthuri23_1, ev_household_income_kiptot11_1]. Brazilian agroforestry viability studies report favourable financial indicators, and diversifying production and income is said to reduce farmers' vulnerability to commodity price volatility [ev_economic_return_ferraz24_1, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_7, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_8, ev_household_income_seghieri19_8]. A systematic review and meta-analysis of sub-Saharan adoption studies, mostly from Ethiopia, Kenya and Malawi, found agroforestry adoption raises household income (Cohen's d = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.13 to 0.44, p < 0.001), from diversified revenue in fruit, timber and fuelwood [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]. In the East Usambara Mountains, Tanzania, cash-crop revenues, especially from cardamom, and total income were significantly higher on farms using improved agroforestry, and gross income per capita was US$ 157 against US$ 74 on traditional farms [ev_household_income_reyes05_1]. In Rwanda, tree products are a safety net: food-insecure farmers more often sold tree products for income than food-secure farmers [ev_household_income_ndoli21_1]. In Nyando District, Kenya, agroforestry-project households sold fuel wood and timber to buy food during the drought, and in Lower Nyando held more livestock wealth than control households [ev_household_income_thorlak12_1, ev_household_income_thorlak12_2]. In a Mozambique carbon-forestry scheme promoting almost exclusively agroforestry, overall household income was generally increased [ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. In the Nepal mid-hills, after a market-oriented agroforestry project of fodder-tree hedgerows and understorey cash crops, bundled with marketing support, training, seed subsidies and organic fertiliser, the share of participating households below the poverty line dropped from 48 % to 34 % and the average farm-income figure rose from 37 to 48 percent, mainly from understorey crops, while off-farm income changed by -9% [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1]. In West Java, Indonesia, agroforestry had a higher net present value and benefit-cost ratio than swidden cultivation, according to a review's reading of Rahman et al. (2017) [ev_economic_return_ntawu23_2].
conditionality: Several units show no effect or a loss: the pooled systematic-review income effect is not statistically significant, Regreening Africa found average tree-product income unchanged and no short-term income change detectable, and some Brazilian system components were loss-making [ev_household_income_castle21s_1, ev_household_income_rgaf23_6, ev_household_income_crs23_5, ev_economic_return_ferraz24_6]. The working paper's revenue measure is gross revenue, not profit, and not significant [ev_economic_return_steward23wp_1]. The Lower Nyando livestock-wealth difference, used by the authors as an income surrogate, was not significant at conventional levels, and the timber-sales finding is farmer-reported [ev_household_income_thorlak12_2, ev_household_income_thorlak12_1]. The Mozambique result is a review citation without an effect size [ev_household_income_lasco14_1]. The Nepal results come from a bundled project and are not credited in full to the trees: they are a before-and-after recall survey of participating households with no control group, and the share of the bundle due to agroforestry is not stated [ev_rural_poverty_pandit19_1, ev_household_income_pandit19_1]. The sub-Saharan pooled income effect rests on adopter versus non-adopter contrasts, many with weak causal identification, and its pool includes payments for ecosystem services in Mozambique, so part of that gain is a cash transfer rather than a production effect [ev_household_income_jemaneh26_1]. The Tanzanian comparison is gross income from a household survey without randomisation: the improved farms bundled trees with cash crops, manure and dairy cattle, were larger and had more off-farm income, and the authors note household overhead costs were also higher [ev_household_income_reyes05_1]. The Indonesian result is second-hand, from a small sample, and compares against swidden cultivation rather than permanent cropland [ev_economic_return_ntawu23_2].

effect_mechanism: In western Kenya, returns to labour from improved fallows were 33 percent higher than from no-input continuous maize, about 87.5% of Lower Nyando farmers who had their trees for 4 years reported income improvements, and a Mozambique PES tree-planting programme significantly raised cash income per capita [ev_economic_return_place05_3, ev_t6_income_timebenefit_castle21_6, ev_household_income_castle21s_6]. In Ethiopia, market-oriented agroforestry with Acacia decurrens is credited with income, employment and reduced poverty in supported microwatersheds [ev_household_income_ieg20_3]. Fertilizer trees limit financial risk in drought years: where a crop fails, farmers using inorganic fertilizer lose the US$164 spent on the input, against US$90 for farmers who planted fertilizer trees [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1]. In southern Malawi, under higher fertiliser prices the value-cost ratio of a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop with maize stayed above 4.0, which the authors call a profitable scenario, while the higher prices pulled monoculture maize down to 2.5 or less [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. On-station and on-farm trials that cost both systems show trees with crops earning more than either alone: in Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping without fertiliser gave a net benefit of US$4148 per hectare against US$2386 for the traditional treeless maize/groundnut intercrop [ev_economic_return_tonye95_1]; in North Kordofan, Sudan, crops grown in an Acacia senegal gum plantation out-earned the same crops grown alone: sorghum gave a net revenue of 558 SDG per hectare against 501 SDG as a sole crop, sesame 300 against 205, and roselle 518 against 389 [ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_fadl13_5, ev_economic_return_fadl13_6]; and in West Bengal, India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system gave net returns 2.66 times those of sole pigeon pea over a 10-year cycle, with a surge in the final year from the Gmelina timber harvest [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1]. In southwestern Nigeria, a sweet orange orchard intercropped with chilli pepper and amaranthus had a net present value of N 154300 and one intercropped with cassava and maize N 105900, against N -37900 for the monocropped orchard, which yielded no revenue in its first years while the intercropped plots earned throughout [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_2, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_3, ev_household_income_aiyel01_4]. Trees can also compensate for crop losses: a review of 74 articles found the share of studies reporting harm fell from 36% for yield to 16% for overall livelihood effects, and where trees raised food yield the livelihood effect was positive in 86% of studies [ev_household_income_reed17_1, ev_household_income_reed17_2, ev_household_income_reed17_3]. In Xinjiang, China, juvenile plumcot intercrops gave a higher average cash flow than sole crops [ev_economic_return_wang23_1].
conditionality: The gains depend on land, labour and input costs, and some adopters lose. In south-western Nigeria, mulching maize with leaves cut and carried from a multipurpose-tree plot gave higher net benefits than nitrogen fertilizer only when the land under the trees was not valued; where land is scarce the technology is unprofitable in both the short and long term [ev_economic_return_korm99_5, ev_economic_return_korm99_6]. In West Bengal the benefit–cost ratio of sole pigeon pea was higher than that of pigeon pea intercropped with Gmelina or mango, so the higher net return came with higher costs [ev_economic_return_biswas22_2]. Several effects did not reach significance or reversed: Zambian improved fallows raised maize income but not total crop income, Kenyan improved fallows changed liquid assets but not significantly, and crop–fruit tree intercropping in China (Dai et al., 2017) lowered gross income [ev_household_income_castle21s_4, ev_household_income_castle21s_5, ev_household_income_castle21s_2]; in western Kenya small farm sizes limited the impact of improved fallows on poverty even though they were attractive to the poor [ev_household_income_place05_2]. Most of the quantified gains are net returns or net present values from research-managed trials, components of household income rather than measured poverty change [ev_economic_return_tonye95_1, ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1]. The Nigerian orchard compares trees with crops against trees alone, so it shows the value of the crops in the alleys rather than of adding trees to a field [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1]. justification.mechanism: In western Kenya, returns to labour from improved fallows were 33 percent higher than from no-input continuous maize, about 87.5% of Lower Nyando farmers who had their trees for 4 years reported income improvements, and a Mozambique PES tree-planting programme significantly raised cash income per capita [ev_economic_return_place05_3, ev_t6_income_timebenefit_castle21_6, ev_household_income_castle21s_6]. In Ethiopia, market-oriented agroforestry with Acacia decurrens is credited with income, employment and reduced poverty in supported microwatersheds [ev_household_income_ieg20_3]. Fertilizer trees limit financial risk in drought years: where a crop fails, farmers using inorganic fertilizer lose the US$164 spent on the input, against US$90 for farmers who planted fertilizer trees [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1]. In southern Malawi, under higher fertiliser prices the value-cost ratio of a Tephrosia vogelii relay intercrop with maize stayed above 4.0, which the authors call a profitable scenario, while the higher prices pulled monoculture maize down to 2.5 or less [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1]. On-station and on-farm trials that cost both systems show trees with crops earning more than either alone: in Cameroon, Leucaena alley cropping without fertiliser gave a net benefit of US$4148 per hectare against US$2386 for the traditional treeless maize/groundnut intercrop [ev_economic_return_tonye95_1]; in North Kordofan, Sudan, crops grown in an Acacia senegal gum plantation out-earned the same crops grown alone: sorghum gave a net revenue of 558 SDG per hectare against 501 SDG as a sole crop, sesame 300 against 205, and roselle 518 against 389 [ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_fadl13_5, ev_economic_return_fadl13_6]; and in West Bengal, India, a Gmelina-mango-pigeon pea system gave net returns 2.66 times those of sole pigeon pea over a 10-year cycle, with a surge in the final year from the Gmelina timber harvest [ev_economic_return_biswas22_1]. In southwestern Nigeria, a sweet orange orchard intercropped with chilli pepper and amaranthus had a net present value of N 154300 and one intercropped with cassava and maize N 105900, against N -37900 for the monocropped orchard, which yielded no revenue in its first years while the intercropped plots earned throughout [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_2, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_3, ev_household_income_aiyel01_4]. Trees can also compensate for crop losses: a review of 74 articles found the share of studies reporting harm fell from 36% for yield to 16% for overall livelihood effects, and where trees raised food yield the livelihood effect was positive in 86% of studies [ev_household_income_reed17_1, ev_household_income_reed17_2, ev_household_income_reed17_3]. In Xinjiang, China, juvenile plumcot intercrops gave a higher average cash flow than sole crops [ev_economic_return_wang23_1].
justification.conditionality: The gains depend on land, labour and input costs, and some adopters lose. In south-western Nigeria, mulching maize with leaves cut and carried from a multipurpose-tree plot gave higher net benefits than nitrogen fertilizer only when the land under the trees was not valued; where land is scarce the technology is unprofitable in both the short and long term [ev_economic_return_korm99_5, ev_economic_return_korm99_6]. In West Bengal the benefit–cost ratio of sole pigeon pea was higher than that of pigeon pea intercropped with Gmelina or mango, so the higher net return came with higher costs [ev_economic_return_biswas22_2]. Several effects did not reach significance or reversed: Zambian improved fallows raised maize income but not total crop income, Kenyan improved fallows changed liquid assets but not significantly, and crop–fruit tree intercropping in China (Dai et al., 2017) lowered gross income [ev_household_income_castle21s_4, ev_household_income_castle21s_5, ev_household_income_castle21s_2]; in western Kenya small farm sizes limited the impact of improved fallows on poverty even though they were attractive to the poor [ev_household_income_place05_2]. Most of the quantified gains are net returns or net present values from research-managed trials, components of household income rather than measured poverty change [ev_economic_return_tonye95_1, ev_economic_return_fadl13_4, ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1]. The Nigerian orchard compares trees with crops against trees alone, so it shows the value of the crops in the alleys rather than of adding trees to a field [ev_economic_return_aiyel01_1]. The Ethiopian unit is an evaluation lesson rather than a measured effect [ev_household_income_ieg20_3]. The Zambian figures are an earlier study cited in an ICRAF working paper and compare losses on crop failure rather than incomes [ev_economic_return_chaudhury11_1]. The Malawian value-cost ratio is a fertiliser-price scenario on on-farm trial data, not measured household income [ev_economic_return_snapp10_1].

effect_mechanism: FMNR and related regeneration-based farmland raise rural household income through tree products and diversified livelihoods. In the Sahel, FMNR adopters who moved from low to continuous practice saw a significant increase in the value of harvested tree products, by about 36% in Burkina Faso, 38% in Mali, 36% in Niger and 34% in the Sahel as a whole [ev_household_income_bina15_3], and moving from low to continuous practice raised gross income per capita by about 13%, and from low to young/new practice by 10% [ev_household_income_bina15_2, ev_household_income_bina15_1]. In Niger, FMNR adoption raised gross annual household income by between 22,805 and 27,950 FCFA (46 to 56 USD) per capita, an 18 to 24% increase, with an estimated annual benefit-cost ratio of 2.5 to 3.0 and a 20-year net present value of €772/ha [ev_household_income_haglund11_1, ev_economic_return_haglund11_1, ev_economic_return_abasse23_1]. Sale of fuelwood and service wood from FMNR is reported to raise income across all social categories, including the very vulnerable [ev_household_income_abasse23_1]; a separate estimate put the annual value of FMNR, through improved soil fertility, firewood, fodder and other products, at US$56 per hectare in Niger [ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_7], and the social return on investment of a Ghanaian FMNR project at US$655-887 per household per year [ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_8]. In Senegal, FMNR-adopting households gained on average 72.65 USD per season from selling non-timber forest products, against 29.73 USD for non-adopters [ev_household_income_seghieri19_12]. In Honduras, farmers using the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system gained a new income stream from renting their land for livestock grazing, because the system produces more stover [ev_household_income_welc02_7]. Across seven project countries, a World Vision meta-analysis found participants 15 percentage points more likely than non-participants to report an increase in household income and nine percentage points more likely to report a decrease in community poverty, an effect reported similarly by poorer households, female-headed households and female respondents [ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5, ev_rural_poverty_wvfmnr19_10]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates farm income increased, noting diversified income from wood, honey, medicinal products and other non-wood products [ev_household_income_wocat_507_2019_farm_income].
conditionality: Against this, the same World Vision multi-country meta-analysis finds Uganda a clear outlier: participant households there were significantly less likely to report income improvements, which the authors attribute partly to participants being poorer households with different income-generation opportunities — the practice worsening the outcome for some adopters, counted here as measured harm [ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_6]. Several Sahel income gains are not statistically significant under the authors' own 5% convention (the 10% and 13% gross-income figures, and the low-to-young tree-product-value gain), though the authors describe them as increases [ev_household_income_bina15_1, ev_household_income_bina15_2, ev_household_income_bina15_4]. The Honduran and Ghanaian/Nigerien World Vision figures are grey-literature project self-evaluations or practitioner articles by project-promoter staff, with a positive-bias discount, and the World Vision brief itself states the FMNR effect cannot be fully disentangled from other project activities [ev_household_income_welc02_7, ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_7, ev_economic_return_wvfmnr19_8, ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5]. All units sit in low and lower-middle-income Sub-Saharan African, South Asian and Southeast Asian contexts (Niger, Burkina Faso, Mali, Senegal, Honduras, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Timor-Leste), in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_household_income_haglund11_1, ev_household_income_bina15_3, ev_household_income_welc02_7, ev_household_income_wvfmnr19_5].

effect_mechanism: Returns to farmers, used here as a proxy for rural poverty, tend to be higher in shaded coffee and cocoa. A meta-analysis found the average net return of shaded systems significantly higher by 23% than conventional systems, with a trend toward a higher benefit-cost ratio (1.66 against 1.44) [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_1, ev_economic_return_jezeer17_2]. Shade also cushions price shocks: in a case cited second-hand, a coffee price crash cut the net revenue of sun-grown coffee far more (30-fold) than of extensive agroforestry (2.9-fold) [ev_economic_return_jezeer17_3], and a farm model for Costa Rica and Guatemala found losses under a 50% coffee price fall were lower for high-shade and diversified systems, with high-shade low-investment farms holding a long-run net present value above zero where low-shade farms averaged one below zero [ev_economic_return_lalani24_2, ev_economic_return_lalani24_1]. In Bolivia the return on labour over the years was, by a cited study, almost twice as high in agroforestry as in monoculture, and in Paraná, Brazil a financial model found net present value and benefit-cost index always higher for shaded coffee [ev_economic_return_dsantos23_7, ev_economic_return_robusti17_1]. Among certified coffee farms in Nicaragua, C.A.F.E. Practices certification was associated with higher net income [ev_economic_return_castle21s_1]. In Rwanda, Tephrosia vogelii grown as mulch within smallholder coffee gave the largest gross margins and returns to labour and the most favourable benefit-cost ratio (5.5) in the first season, from higher coffee yield and less weeding labour [ev_economic_return_bucagu13_4].
conditionality: The row carries a harm signal: in a farm survey in Guayas, Ecuador, technified monoculture earned the best net margin per hectare ($2323) against $1565 for organic and $484 for traditional cacao agroforestry [ev_economic_return_perezneira16_1, ev_economic_return_perezneira16_2]. Other units find no difference: a pan-tropical cocoa meta-analysis found higher total system production not reflected in higher revenues or net present values [ev_economic_return_niether20_1, ev_household_income_niether20_1], and after Hurricane Stan coffee management had no effect on economic losses in Mexico [ev_economic_return_philpott08_1]. What separates the sides is the comparison: the gains are against sun-grown or low-shade systems and under price shocks, while the losses are against an input-intensive technified monoculture. The certification result is bundled, crediting a certification scheme rather than shade alone [ev_economic_return_castle21s_1], the price-fall and net-present-value comparisons are modelled [ev_economic_return_lalani24_1, ev_economic_return_robusti17_1], and the Bolivian labour-return figure is read second-hand [ev_economic_return_dsantos23_7]. The Rwandan result is from the first, unfertilised season of an on-farm trial, and Tephrosia there is a cut-back mulch shrub rather than a shade tree [ev_economic_return_bucagu13_4]. All units are crop-specific to coffee or cocoa except the Bolivian one, and the evidence mostly comes from upper-middle- and lower-middle-income producing countries, with low-income Rwanda the exception; returns are proxies for poverty, not poverty itself.

effect_mechanism: A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry five and ten times better than controls for runoff and soil loss respectively [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis found agroforestry trees reduced soil erosion by 50% against crop monocultures, and stated mechanisms include greater soil cover and structure protecting against raindrop impact, roots aiding infiltration and reducing surface runoff, and live fences lowering runoff velocity; runoff reduction is used as a component [ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_santos25_2, ev_runoff_reduction_watts22_2, ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_5]. A review compiling published field studies of agroforestry against its controls found average soil-loss reductions of 68% for silvopastoral systems, 66% for silvoarable agroforestry and 55% for linear tree plantings, with no significant difference among the system types, and average water-loss reductions of 73% for silvopastoral and 43% for silvoarable systems [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_1, ev_runoff_reduction_zhu19_2]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT compiler adds that, due to less wind and water erosion, the siltation of ponds and water pans is reduced [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. In Lower Nyando, Kenya, farmers reported that tree roots prevented extensive soil erosion and soil fertility loss during the floods [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. During Hurricane Mitch in October 1998, Honduran farmers practising the Quesungual system suffered less landslide damage than those using traditional slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1]. In Costa Rica and Nicaragua, runoff equalled 28-48% of rainfall on pastures without trees against less than 10% in silvopastoral systems [ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1]. Runoff was higher on grass pasture than in tree-dominated fodder banks, so tree cover attenuates runoff and the soil erosion it causes [ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. Within single sub-practices, live fences of Gliricidia sepium are used to prevent erosion, shade trees attenuate runoff and erosion by close to a factor of two against full-sun plots, and in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion erosion under silvopasture was 35.3 percent lower than on degraded pasture soils [ev_erosion_hazard_moran18_2, ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1]. In shaded perennial systems, a study on a Costa Rican coffee farm found shade trees reduced sheet erosion by a factor of 2 against full-sun plots [ev_erosion_hazard_seghieri19_1], and after Hurricane Stan in Chiapas, Mexico, coffee farms with more complex vegetation suffered less landslide damage [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_10]. Along field boundaries, on Saskatchewan prairie fields with old shelterbelts planted to reduce wind erosion, erosion midway between the belts has generally been much less than in unsheltered fields, judged from depth to carbonates and 137Cs, and the authors expect soil productivity there to be higher than in open fields [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report that soil erosion has been nearly stopped, and estimate nutrient loss through erosion at more than 10 times lower than under slash-and-burn [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4].
conditionality: The class is moderate because it is set by a vote across sub-practices: the cross-family, planted silvoarable and silvopastoral cells read as strong reductions, linear boundary plantings as moderate, and regeneration-based farmland and shaded perennial systems as slight. The cross-practice syntheses agree on large reductions: the sub-Saharan and pantropical meta-analyses and the review of compiled field studies, whose averages hold across silvopastoral, silvoarable and linear plantings alike [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_muchane20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_2, ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_3]. Single-practice field evidence is often weaker than those averages, so the size a project can expect depends on site and practice [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The compiled-review percentages are simple averages of study reductions, not weighted meta-analytic effects, and they mix temperate and tropical studies [ev_erosion_hazard_zhu19_1]. The shade-tree effect represents little at catchment scale on the andisols studied [ev_runoff_reduction_seghieri19_3]. Site matters within a practice: erosion fell 35.3 percent in Colombia's Coffee Ecoregion but only 5.4 percent in the Cesar River Valley [ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_1, ev_erosion_hazard_cmscr20_2]. The sub-Saharan authors warn the very large effect sizes could reflect publication bias and expect more modest effects with more studies [ev_erosion_hazard_kuyah19_1]. Regreening Africa observed no large overall change in erosion prevalence and found no link between more trees on farm and lower erosion, the FMNR result is participants' reported erosion, and the Nicaraguan hurricane result bundles trees with terraces and contour planting [ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_3, ev_erosion_hazard_rgaf23_5, ev_erosion_hazard_wvfmnr19_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_9]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not an erosion measurement, and the siltation rating enters as a component [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_507_2019_downstream_siltation]. The Lower Nyando erosion finding is farmer-reported, not measured [ev_erosion_hazard_thorlak12_1]. The landslide and runoff results are earlier studies cited in a working paper, a CATIE edited volume and a Spanish-language review; the runoff units enter as components of erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_chaudhury11_1, ev_runoff_reduction_montagnini15_1, ev_runoff_reduction_cisneros24_1]. The Chiapas landslide results are crop-specific coffee evidence from a single hurricane, with the landslide-volume and landslide-size trends only marginal (P = 0.062) and no effect of nearby forest cover [ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_3, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_5, ev_erosion_hazard_philpott08_4]. The Honduran erosion claim is a narrative from a promoter-written grey-literature article with no measured erosion rate, and the effect belongs to the whole bundle of trees, mulch cover, zero tillage and no burning [ev_erosion_hazard_welc02_4]. The Saskatchewan shelterbelt unit is high-income temperate evidence from Canada, outside the LIC/LMIC target; it infers past erosion from soil markers and states no erosion rate [ev_erosion_hazard_kowa95_5].

effect_mechanism: The measured evidence splits on whether trees add water the system can use or compete with crops for it, and the separator is usually which water measure is used — system water-use efficiency (biomass per unit of water used, which counts the tree's own biomass) versus the crop's own soil moisture. In Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised millet's rainwater-use efficiency by 17 to 47% depending on fertiliser treatment, and raised the millet/cowpea intercrop's water-use efficiency by 11 to 17% [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. In Malawi, a long-running gliricidia agroforestry trial found system water-use efficiency (total above-ground biomass, including the tree, per unit of seasonal water use) strongly and significantly higher in every season for gliricidia-based systems than for sole maize or maize-pigeonpea, by a wide margin (for example 1.43-1.97 g/kg for gliricidia+maize against 0.15-0.54 g/kg for sole maize) [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5]. In Honduras, the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system retained 15% more soil water in the driest month than slash-and-burn (23% against 8% humidity), equivalent to about 20 mm of extra rainfall and 20 more days a crop could survive without rain, attributed to better infiltration through soil cover and higher organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry improved both infiltration and soil moisture content compared with controls [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. A continental-scale model finds rainfall dependent on upwind tree cover by 10 to 20%, rising with more tree cover and falling with upwind deforestation [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates water availability increased, attributing it to greater water retention raising groundwater levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability].
conditionality: Set against this, when the same Malawi trial measures the crop's own soil moisture rather than system water-use efficiency, the sign often reverses: available soil water at the start of the cropping season was generally lower in the tree-based systems, consistent with trees depleting moisture through the dry season, and the decline from March to August was most pronounced in the gliricidia-based treatments; volumetric moisture was significantly lower under the gliricidia+maize+pigeonpea system at depth in one season reading and slightly lower in another, though a later-season reading found it significantly greater at depth, and the authors' overall conclusion is that pruned gliricidia does not create undue water competition under Malawi's rainfall, several season-level contrasts showing no significant difference [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]. In Ghana and across a ten-country cocoa meta-analysis, shaded cocoa and cocoa agroforestry measured significantly lower soil water than full-sun or monoculture systems, attributed to combined shade-tree and crop transpiration raising water uptake [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. In Ethiopia, subsoil moisture was lowest for wheat grown with Faidherbia albida, intermediate for sole tree and highest in the open field, though topsoil moisture showed no difference [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2].
