justification.mechanism: The measured evidence splits on whether trees add water the system can use or compete with crops for it, and the separator is usually which water measure is used — system water-use efficiency (biomass per unit of water used, which counts the tree's own biomass) versus the crop's own soil moisture. In Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees raised millet's rainwater-use efficiency by 17 to 47% depending on fertiliser treatment, and raised the millet/cowpea intercrop's water-use efficiency by 11 to 17% [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. In Malawi, a long-running gliricidia agroforestry trial found system water-use efficiency (total above-ground biomass, including the tree, per unit of seasonal water use) strongly and significantly higher in every season for gliricidia-based systems than for sole maize or maize-pigeonpea, by a wide margin (for example 1.43-1.97 g/kg for gliricidia+maize against 0.15-0.54 g/kg for sole maize) [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5]. In Honduras, the Quesungual slash-and-mulch system retained 15% more soil water in the driest month than slash-and-burn (23% against 8% humidity), equivalent to about 20 mm of extra rainfall and 20 more days a crop could survive without rain, attributed to better infiltration through soil cover and higher organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. A sub-Saharan meta-analysis found agroforestry improved both infiltration and soil moisture content compared with controls [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. A continental-scale model finds rainfall dependent on upwind tree cover by 10 to 20%, rising with more tree cover and falling with upwind deforestation [ev_water_regulation_vannoordwijk21_4]. A WOCAT compiler for Kenyan FMNR rates water availability increased, attributing it to greater water retention raising groundwater levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability].
justification.conditionality: Set against this, when the same Malawi trial measures the crop's own soil moisture rather than system water-use efficiency, the sign often reverses: available soil water at the start of the cropping season was generally lower in the tree-based systems, consistent with trees depleting moisture through the dry season, and the decline from March to August was most pronounced in the gliricidia-based treatments; volumetric moisture was significantly lower under the gliricidia+maize+pigeonpea system at depth in one season reading and slightly lower in another, though a later-season reading found it significantly greater at depth, and the authors' overall conclusion is that pruned gliricidia does not create undue water competition under Malawi's rainfall, several season-level contrasts showing no significant difference [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]. On the Canadian prairies, soil water near an old shelterbelt dropped noticeably in one year, tentatively attributed to uptake by the trees and grasses in the preceding fallow year [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. In Mexican coffee, high-shade sites showed smaller day-to-day swings in soil water from evaporation than low-shade sites, a buffering benefit rather than a higher measured moisture level, since shaded sites also gained less water after rain through canopy interception [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]; a German alley-cropping trial in a drought year found soil water lower on the open field than under trees, though not significant at every position [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. effect_mechanism: Only two temperate field studies sit in this high-income row, and they point in opposite directions. In a German alley-cropping trial in a drought year, soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system, though differences were not significant for all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. Beside Saskatchewan field shelterbelts, spring soil water content in 1990 dropped noticeably from 0.1 to 0.05 relative distance from the belt, which the authors put down, tentatively, to uptake by the trees and grasses in the previous fallow year; in 1989 the pattern differed, with a slight trend of decreasing available water from the field edge to the centre [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. The first reads as less water stress with trees, the second as more water stress next to them.
conditionality: The two units differ in practice, year and position, so they do not contradict each other directly: the German comparison is alley cropping against an open field in a drought year, while the Canadian study compares soil close to a shelterbelt with soil further into the same field [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1, ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. Neither measures crop water stress itself; both measure soil water as a component of it. The German differences were not significant at all positions [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1], and the Canadian drop appeared in 1990, not in 1989, and its cause is hedged [ev_soil_moisture_kowa95_7]. Both are high-income temperate sites (Germany, Canada), outside the LIC/LMIC target. Missing: further studies of each practice, and any measure of crop water stress.

effect_mechanism: The measured soil-water evidence points both ways, and timing and soil depth separate the sides. On the side of more soil water, a sub-Saharan meta-analysis finds that agroforestry improved infiltration and soil moisture content compared to the control (RR 1.6 for soil moisture, with 70% of soil-moisture observations above RR 1) [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1]. In a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration and reduced soil evaporation under greater ground cover [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10], and in the second season's May water content in that system was much greater than in all other treatments at depths below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]. Water use efficiency was also higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.97 against 0.15 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1998/99 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. In Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees in the cropped block increased the rainwater use efficiency of millet by 17 and 47 % with farmyard manure and in the unfertilised control, and that of the millet/cowpea intercrop by 11 to 17 % [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. On the side of less soil water, under Faidherbia albida parkland in Ethiopia soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; in cocoa, a pan-tropical meta-analysis found soils under agroforestry significantly lower in volumetric water content than under full-sun monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]; in a Ghanaian cocoa field, the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa resulted in higher water uptake and less soil water than under full sun [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]; at Makoka the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests that the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. Trees therefore draw down dry-season and subsoil water, while recharge-season soil water and whole-system water productivity favour them. Several measurements found no difference: topsoil moisture did not vary under Faidherbia [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2], and at Makoka the distribution of water in the profile was generally comparable in all cropping systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_1], with no significant treatment effects in the second season, in the second season's October, or in December and January of the third season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_6, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_7, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_9]; the authors conclude that gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season does not provoke undue competition for water with associated crops [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet adds increased water availability, its compiler crediting an increase in water retention which increases the ground water levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. In Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report 23% soil humidity in the driest month (April) against 8% in a traditional slash-and-burn field, a difference equivalent to 20mm of rainfall, or 20 more days that crops can be sustained without rain; they explain it by better infiltration through the soil cover and more soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1].
conditionality: Within low- and lower-middle-income evidence the sides still disagree: the sub-Saharan meta-analysis, the Malawi Gliricidia trial and the Niger Ziziphus trial point to less water stress, while the Faidherbia subsoil depletion in Ethiopia and the cocoa soil-water deficits in the meta-analysis and in Ghana point to more [ev_soil_water_retention_kuyah19_1, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. The separator is timing and depth: trees deplete soil water through the dry season and below the topsoil, so less may be available when the crop is sown, while recharge-season water and system water productivity favour the tree plots [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4, ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10]. Management matters: the Malawi conclusion holds for gliricidia pruned before and during the cropping season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_11], and the Ethiopian parkland trees were heavily pruned on farmers' fields [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]. The Makoka water use efficiency figures are total above-ground biomass of the whole system, trees and crops together, per unit of seasonal water use, not grain per unit of water [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1]; the tree biomass inflates the tree-system figures, and the authors caution that soil evaporation and water-table uptake were not measured, so the gap is probably overstated. The Niger figures are crop biomass per unit of rainfall, from a trial with the trees in a single block and the tree-free comparison in a separate block, so tree presence was not randomised and the contrast carries block effects [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. The Makoka units therefore count here, for water stress, and are held out of the production gap because they say nothing about crop yield. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet, not a soil-moisture measurement, and stays on water access rather than soil moisture [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. Infiltration and groundwater-recharge findings for catchments are carried in the agroforestry catchment water yield rows. The cocoa units are crop-specific and do not measure crop water stress directly; the Ghanaian study is a single farm with shade trees of Albizia ferruginea and Antiaris toxicaria [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. The Honduran soil-humidity figures come from a grey-literature article by the project's own promoters, report no replication or significance, and compare a bundle (trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning) against slash-and-burn, so the trees cannot be credited alone [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1].

effect_mechanism: In tree-crop systems, shade and tree water use change soil moisture in opposing ways. A multi-country meta-analysis of cocoa agroforestry across Ghana, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Indonesia, Malaysia, Costa Rica, Panama, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia found soils under agroforestry have a significantly lower volumetric water content than under monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. In Ghana, the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa plants raised water uptake, with a consequent reduction in soil water compared with full-sun cocoa [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. Against this, in a Mexican coffee lysimeter study, soil water losses and gains fluctuated far more at the low-shade site than at the medium- and high-shade sites, showing that shade can buffer soil moisture loss through evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3].
conditionality: This row rolls up all tree-perennial farming-system evidence regardless of sub-practice family; in practice all three units come from shaded perennial-crop systems (cocoa, coffee). Most of the units measure less soil water under shade — the multi-country cocoa meta-analysis and the Ghana study — so the class is a slight increase in water stress rather than a benefit, and the Mexican coffee buffering result is the one offsetting signal, which keeps agreement at high rather than a stronger reading [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. None of the three states a size for the difference, and none measures a drought or other named water-stress hazard — all describe ordinary dry-season soil moisture [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The Mexican result is a slower rate of loss and smaller swings under shade, not a higher measured moisture level, and the same site gained less water after rain through canopy interception [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The cocoa evidence sits in lower- and upper-middle-income countries across Latin America, West Africa and Southeast Asia, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3].

justification.mechanism: The direction comes mainly from a Gliricidia + maize trial at Makoka, Malawi, now joined by a Ziziphus trial in the Sahel. Water use efficiency was higher in the tree systems in every season, for example 1.97 against 0.15 g of biomass per kg of water for gliricidia + maize against sole maize in 1998/99, and 2.41 against 0.87 for gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea against maize + pigeonpea in 1999/00 [ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_2, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_3, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_4, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_5, ev_rain_water_productivity_chirwa07_6]. Available water content tended to be greater in the gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea system at the peak of the recharge phase, which the authors attribute to increased infiltration from improved soil structure and reduced soil evaporation under greater ground cover [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_10], and in the second season's May that system held much more water than all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_8]. In Niger, Ziziphus mauritiana trees in the cropped block increased the rainwater use efficiency of millet by 17 and 47 % with farmyard manure and in the unfertilised control, and that of the millet/cowpea intercrop by 17 % in the control and by 11 % with manure on millet and SSP1 on cowpea [ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_1, ev_rain_water_productivity_bado21_2]. A German alley-cropping trial in a drought year adds that soil water content remained lower on the open field than in the alley-cropping system [ev_soil_water_retention_majaura25_1]. The same Malawi trial also records harm: the lower available soil water at the beginning of the cropping season in the tree-based systems suggests the trees continued to deplete moisture during the dry season [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_2], the March-to-August decline was most pronounced in the tree-based systems [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_3], water content was slightly lower under gliricidia + maize in the dry season when the trees were left unpruned [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_5], and in the first season's May water content under gliricidia + maize + pigeonpea was lower than in all other treatments below 60 cm [ev_soil_moisture_chirwa07_4]. effect_mechanism: Studies of trees on regenerated farmland disagree on soil water, so no direction is stated. On the side of more water stress, under Faidherbia albida parkland in Ethiopia soil moisture in the sub-soil was the least for wheat with tree, intermediate for sole tree and the highest for open field, while the authors observed no variation in topsoil moisture content between treatments [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1, ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_2]. On the side of less, in Lempira, Honduras, promoters of the Quesungual system report 23% soil humidity in the driest month (April) against 8% in a traditional slash-and-burn field, a difference equivalent to 20mm of rainfall, or 20 more days that crops can be sustained without rain; they explain it by better infiltration through the soil cover and more soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. The Kenyan FMNR WOCAT sheet also points that way, its compiler crediting an increase in water retention which increases the ground water levels [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability].
conditionality: The sides differ in system and in what is measured. The Ethiopian result is a measured subsoil draw-down under heavily pruned parkland trees with a growing wheat crop [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]; the Honduran result is driest-month soil humidity in a slash-and-mulch system against slash-and-burn, which the authors credit to soil cover and soil organic matter [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]; and the WOCAT unit speaks of groundwater, not crop-root-zone moisture [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. The Honduran soil-humidity figures come from a grey-literature article by the project's own promoters, report no replication or significance, and compare a bundle (trees with mulch, zero tillage and no burning) against slash-and-burn, so the trees cannot be credited alone [ev_soil_moisture_welc02_1]. The WOCAT unit is a compiler judgement on a documented technology sheet rather than a soil-moisture measurement [ev_water_access_deficit_wocat_507_2019_water_availability]. Whether pruning or tree density changes the subsoil draw-down is not tested [ev_soil_water_retention_sida18_1]. The cited parkland tree-density result for groundwater recharge sits in the regeneration catchment water yield row.

justification.statement: agroforestry water_stress: CONFLICTING EVIDENCE — material weight on both the benefit and the harm side, so no direction is stated. This is not a null finding: studies found real effects, in opposite directions, and the agreement note lists both sides. Read the conditionality for what separates them (transfer: in_context).

effect_mechanism: In tree-crop systems, shade and tree water use change soil moisture in opposing ways. A multi-country meta-analysis of cocoa agroforestry across Ghana, Cameroon, Côte d'Ivoire, Indonesia, Malaysia, Costa Rica, Panama, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia found soils under agroforestry have a significantly lower volumetric water content than under monocultures [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1]. In Ghana, the combined transpiration of shade trees and cocoa plants raised water uptake, with a consequent reduction in soil water compared with full-sun cocoa [ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2]. Against this, in a Mexican coffee lysimeter study, soil water losses and gains fluctuated far more at the low-shade site than at the medium- and high-shade sites, showing that shade can buffer soil moisture loss through evaporation [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3].
conditionality: This is the shaded perennial-crop family's own row; cocoa and coffee are this family's crops, so the same three units apply directly. Most of the units measure less soil water under shade — the multi-country cocoa meta-analysis and the Ghana study — so the class is a slight increase in water stress rather than a benefit, and the Mexican coffee buffering result is the one offsetting signal, which keeps agreement at high rather than a stronger reading [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. None of the three states a size for the difference, and none measures a drought or other named water-stress hazard — all describe ordinary dry-season soil moisture [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The Mexican result is a slower rate of loss and smaller swings under shade, not a higher measured moisture level, and the same site gained less water after rain through canopy interception [ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3]. The cocoa evidence sits in lower- and upper-middle-income countries across Latin America, West Africa and Southeast Asia, in context with the LIC/LMIC target [ev_soil_water_retention_niether20_1, ev_soil_moisture_abdul18_2, ev_soil_moisture_lin07_3].
